west-sumatra.s: West Sumatra is a province of Indonesia on the western coast of Sumatra, with its capital at Padang. It is the homeland of the Minangkabau, a matrilineal Muslim people, and earlier held the centres of the Malayu kingdom of Dharmasraya and the kingdom of Adityawarman.

west-banas-river.s: The West Banas is a river of western India that rises in the Aravalli hills of southern Rajasthan and flows south-west through northern Gujarat into the Little Rann of Kutch. It gives its name to Banaskantha district, 'the bank of the Banas', where small princely states such…

worcestershire.s: Worcestershire is a county in the West Midlands of England, with its county town at Worcester on the River Severn. The salt springs of Droitwich made it important from prehistoric times, and it formed the core of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the Hwicce, whose bishopric at…

william-gopallawa.s: William Gopallawa was the last Governor-General of Ceylon, from 1962, and the first President of Sri Lanka, from 1972 to 1978. A lawyer and civil servant from Matale who had served as ambassador to China and the United States, he became the ceremonial head of state when the…

william-massey.s: William Massey was Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1912 until his death in 1925. Leader of the Reform Party, which drew its support from farmers, he used special constables to break the waterfront strike of 1913, led the country through the First World War and signed the…

west-nusa-tenggara.s: West Nusa Tenggara is a province of Indonesia made up of the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa, with its capital at Mataram on Lombok. Formed in 1958, it includes the lands of the former sultanates of Sumbawa, Dompu and Bima.

wenzhou.s: Wenzhou is a port city in southern Zhejiang province, China, on the Ou River near the East China Sea. Its area was the centre of the Dong'ou kingdom of the Yue peoples in the 2nd century BCE, and the city became a trading port under the Song dynasty.

wang-jun-pengzu.s: Wang Jun, courtesy name Pengzu, was a Western Jin governor and general who controlled Youzhou in north-eastern China in the early 4th century. Allied by marriage with the Duan Xianbei, he used Duan and Wuhuan cavalry against the Han Zhao state founded by the Xiongnu.

witigis.s: Witigis was king of the Ostrogoths in Italy from 536 to 540. Raised to the throne after King Theodahad failed against the Byzantine invasion, he ceded Provence and the Ostrogothic protectorate over the Alemanni to the Franks to win their support.

william-iron-arm.s: William Iron Arm was the eldest son of Tancred of Hauteville and the first leader of the Normans in Apulia. Having fought for the Byzantines in Sicily under George Maniakes, where by tradition his single combat with the emir of Syracuse earned him his nickname, he was elected…

william-ii-duke-of-bavaria.s: William II was Duke of Bavaria-Straubing from 1404 to 1417 and, as William VI, Count of Holland, Zeeland and Hainaut. A son of Duke Albert I, he governed mainly from the Low Countries, where the Hook and Cod factions divided Holland.

wupper.s: The Wupper is a river in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, a right tributary of the Rhine about 115 kilometres long. Its valley in the Bergisches Land was one of the earliest industrial regions of Germany, with textile bleaching, dyeing and metalworking.

wenceslaus-i-duke-of-bohemia.s: Wenceslaus I, known as Saint Wenceslas, was Duke of Bohemia from about 921. He promoted Christianity and accepted the overlordship of the German king Henry the Fowler.

war-of-the-breton-succession.s: The War of the Breton Succession was fought from 1341 to 1364 for the Duchy of Brittany between Charles of Blois, backed by France, and John of Montfort and his son, backed by England. Part of the wider Hundred Years' War, it included the Combat of the Thirty in 1351.

wenceslaus-iii-adam-duke-of-cieszyn.n: Wenceslaus III Adam, Duke of Cieszyn
wenceslaus-iii-adam-duke-of-cieszyn.s: Wenceslaus III Adam was a Piast Duke of Cieszyn who succeeded as a child in 1528 and ruled in person from 1545. He introduced the Lutheran Reformation into the duchy and issued a church ordinance for it, and Protestantism remained strong in Cieszyn Silesia despite the later…

war-of-the-julich-succession.s: The War of the Jülich Succession was a dispute over the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg after the death of the childless Duke John William in 1609. Brandenburg and Palatinate-Neuburg, backed by Protestant and Catholic allies, contested the inheritance, which nearly set…

wesel.s: Wesel is a town in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, where the Lippe joins the Rhine. A Hanseatic town in the Duchy of Cleves, it became a refuge for Dutch Calvinists in the 16th century and later a major Prussian fortress.

william-sanchez-of-gascony.s: William Sánchez was Duke of Gascony from about 961 until about 997. He defeated Viking raiders, traditionally at the Battle of Taller around 982, founded the abbey of Saint-Sever in 988 and, after inheriting the county of Bordeaux, made it the ducal seat.

william-viii-duke-of-aquitaine.s: William VIII, born Guy-Geoffrey, was Duke of Aquitaine and Count of Poitou from 1058 to 1086. A son of William V the Great, he secured the Duchy of Gascony in the 1050s and 1060s, uniting it with Aquitaine and extending ducal lordship from the Loire to the Pyrenees.

wladyslaw-the-white.s: Władysław the White was the last Duke of Gniewkowo, of the Kuyavian branch of the Piast dynasty. In 1363 he sold his duchy to King Casimir III and left on pilgrimage, later becoming a monk.

wieliczka.s: Wieliczka is a town in southern Poland, just south-east of Kraków, known for its rock-salt mine. Salt was extracted there from the 13th century, and together with nearby Bochnia the mine was a major source of revenue for the Polish crown for centuries.

wloclawek.s: Włocławek is a city in central Poland on the Vistula, in the historical region of Kuyavia. From the 12th century it was the seat of the bishops of Kuyavia, whose Gothic cathedral still dominates the town.

waleran-iii-duke-of-limburg.s: Waleran III (d. 1226) was Duke of Limburg from 1221, a son of Duke Henry III of Limburg.

wartislaw-i-duke-of-pomerania.s: Wartislaw I (fl. 1120s–1130s) was the first historically attested Duke of Pomerania and ancestor of the Griffin dynasty.

wolgast.s: Wolgast is a town in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Germany, on the Peenestrom opposite the island of Usedom. From 1295 it was the residence of the dukes of Pomerania-Wolgast, whose castle no longer survives.

wladyslaw-ii-of-plock.s: Władysław II of Płock was a Piast duke of Masovia who ruled the lands of Płock, Rawa, Gostynin and neighbouring districts jointly with his elder brother Siemowit VI from 1455. Both brothers died young in early 1462, Władysław in February, without heirs.

william-duke-of-saxe-weimar.s: William was Duke of Saxe-Weimar from 1620 until his death in 1662. A Protestant commander in the early Thirty Years' War, he was captured at the Battle of Stadtlohn in 1623 and later made peace with the emperor.

wittenberg.s: Wittenberg, officially Lutherstadt Wittenberg, is a town on the Elbe in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. It was the seat of the Ascanian dukes of Saxe-Wittenberg and then of the Wettin electors of Saxony, whose University of Wittenberg was founded in 1502.

weimar.s: Weimar is a city in Thuringia, Germany, the residence of the dukes of Saxe-Weimar and later Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach. Around 1800 it became the centre of German literature, home to Goethe, Schiller, Herder and Wieland.

william-ernest-grand-duke-of-saxe-weimar.n: William Ernest, Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach
william-ernest-grand-duke-of-saxe-weimar.s: William Ernest was the last Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, reigning from 1901 until the German Revolution. He was an unpopular, authoritarian ruler, though Weimar's art school and the reformist designer Henry van de Velde flourished under his patronage.

weissenfels.s: Weissenfels is a town on the Saale river in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. From the late seventeenth century it was the residence of the dukes of Saxe-Weissenfels, whose court was known for music and opera.

wroclaw.s: Wrocław (German Breslau) is the largest city of Silesia, on the Oder river in south-western Poland. A bishopric from 1000 and the capital of the Piast dukes of Silesia, it later belonged to Bohemia and the Habsburgs before Prussia took it in 1742.

wurzburg.s: Würzburg is a city on the Main river in Lower Franconia, Bavaria. Saint Boniface founded its bishopric in 742, and its prince-bishops ruled a large territory until 1803.

wiltshire.s: Wiltshire is a landlocked county of southern England, largely made up of the chalk downland of Salisbury Plain. It contains the prehistoric monuments of Stonehenge and Avebury, a World Heritage Site, and many Iron Age hillforts.

willem-piso.s: Willem Piso was a Dutch physician and naturalist from Leiden who served as personal physician to Johan Maurits in Dutch Brazil from 1638 to 1644. He studied tropical diseases and local remedies, including ipecacuanha, and is regarded as a founder of tropical medicine.

willem-adriaan-van-der-stel.s: Willem Adriaan van der Stel succeeded his father Simon van der Stel as governor of the Dutch Cape Colony, serving from 1699 to 1707. He and other officials used their positions to build up large private farms, notably his estate of Vergelegen, and to dominate the colony's…

walter-de-burgh-1st-earl-of-ulster.n: Walter de Burgh, 1st Earl of Ulster
walter-de-burgh-1st-earl-of-ulster.s: Walter de Burgh was an Anglo-Irish lord who held the lordship of Connacht and was created Earl of Ulster by Henry III's son Lord Edward in 1263 or 1264, after the death of Hugh de Lacy. His family became the most powerful in Ireland, and his son Richard, the Red Earl, extended…

waiofar.s: Waiofar was Duke of Aquitaine from 745 to 768, the son of Hunald and grandson of Odo the Great. He defended his duchy's independence against the Carolingian king Pippin the Short, who from 760 led almost yearly campaigns into Aquitaine.

wang-dao.s: Wang Dao was a Chinese statesman of the Wang clan of Langya who guided the founding of the Eastern Jin dynasty. He advised Sima Rui to move to Jianye in 307, won over the gentry families of the lower Yangtze, and served as chief minister under the first three Eastern Jin…

wang-xizhi.s: Wang Xizhi was a Chinese calligrapher of the Eastern Jin dynasty, revered as the 'Sage of Calligraphy'. A member of the powerful Wang clan of Langya, he served as an official in Kuaiji.

wangcheng.s: Wangcheng, the 'Royal City', was the seat of the Zhou kings near modern Luoyang in Henan during much of the Eastern Zhou period. Traditionally founded by the Duke of Zhou as part of the eastern capital, it later became the centre of the small Duchy of Western Zhou.

wahhabism.s: Wahhabism is the Sunni Islamic reform movement founded by Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab in 18th-century Najd, in central Arabia. It calls for a return to strict monotheism and rejects the veneration of saints and tombs.

westo.s: The Westo were an Iroquoian-speaking people who appeared in Virginia and Carolina in the mid-17th century, probably descendants of the Erie. Armed with guns obtained from Virginian traders, they raided other native peoples for captives to sell as slaves.

wirtschaftswunder.s: The Wirtschaftswunder, or economic miracle, was the rapid reconstruction and growth of the West German economy after the currency reform of 1948. Helped by Marshall Plan aid, the social market economy of Ludwig Erhard and strong export demand, output rose quickly, unemployment…

war-of-canudos.s: The War of Canudos was a conflict between the Brazilian Republic and the religious community of Canudos in the backlands of Bahia, founded by the preacher Antônio Conselheiro. The settlement, which grew to many thousands of poor followers, defeated three military expeditions…

washington-luis.s: Washington Luís was a Brazilian politician from São Paulo who served as president of Brazil from 1926 to 1930, the last president of the First Brazilian Republic. Known for his road-building, he broke the alternation of power between São Paulo and Minas Gerais by backing the…

wuwei.s: Wuwei is a city in Gansu province in north-western China, on the eastern part of the Hexi Corridor. Under the Han dynasty it became a commandery on the route to Central Asia, and as Guzang it was the capital of the Former Liang, Later Liang, Southern Liang and Northern Liang…

wei-zhuang.s: Wei Zhuang was a Chinese poet of the late Tang dynasty, celebrated for his ci lyrics and for the long narrative poem Lament of the Lady of Qin, which describes the sack of Chang'an by Huang Chao's rebels in 881. After passing the imperial examinations in 894 he went to…

wornitz.s: The Wörnitz is a river in Bavaria which rises near Schillingsfürst and flows south past Dinkelsbühl, Wassertrüdingen and Oettingen, crossing the Nördlinger Ries crater, to join the Danube at Donauwörth. Several medieval towns, among them the free imperial city of Dinkelsbühl,…

wertach.s: The Wertach is a river in Bavarian Swabia which rises in the Allgäu Alps and flows north through Kaufbeuren to join the Lech at Augsburg. Its valley carried the old road from Augsburg into the Alps, and Kaufbeuren grew at a crossing on its banks.

wissembourg-abbey.s: Wissembourg Abbey was a Benedictine monastery in northern Alsace on the river Lauter, founded in the 7th century and dedicated to Saints Peter and Paul. Richly endowed by Frankish kings, it was a centre of learning where the monk Otfrid wrote his Old High German Gospel Harmony…

wangen-im-allgau.s: Wangen im Allgäu is a town in the Allgäu region of Baden-Württemberg which grew from a settlement under the Abbey of Saint Gall and became a free imperial city in the 13th century. It remained Catholic during the Reformation, passed to Bavaria in 1802 and to Württemberg in…

weil-der-stadt.s: Weil der Stadt is a small town west of Stuttgart in Baden-Württemberg, on the river Würm. A Hohenstaufen possession, it became a free imperial city in the 13th century and kept that status until 1803, when it passed to Württemberg.

wurm-nagold.s: The Würm is a river in Baden-Württemberg that rises south-west of Stuttgart and flows north-west through Weil der Stadt to join the Nagold at Pforzheim. Its valley crosses the Heckengäu, a limestone plateau west of Stuttgart, and several small medieval towns grew along its…

weissenburg-in-bayern.s: Weißenburg in Bayern is a town in Middle Franconia, Bavaria, beside the Roman fort of Biriciana on the Raetian Limes. It was a free imperial city from the Middle Ages until 1802, long rivalled by the margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach in the Wülzburg fortress above it, and…

wulzburg.s: The Wülzburg is a Renaissance fortress on a hill above Weißenburg in Bavaria, built from 1588 by the margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach on the site of a Benedictine abbey. Its five bastions make it one of the best-preserved Renaissance fortresses in Germany, and in the First…

walter-gropius.s: Walter Gropius was a German architect who founded the Bauhaus school in Weimar in 1919 and designed its new building in Dessau in 1925–1926. A pioneer of modern architecture using glass curtain walls and industrial materials, he left Nazi Germany in 1934, worked in England and…

wilhelmshaven.s: Wilhelmshaven is a port city on the Jade Bight on the North Sea coast of Lower Saxony. Founded by Prussia as a naval base on land bought from Oldenburg in 1853 and named after King William I in 1869, it became the main North Sea base of the German navy.

weser.s: The Weser is a river of north-western Germany, formed at Hann. Münden by the confluence of the Werra and the Fulda and flowing about 450 km north through Lower Saxony past Minden and Bremen to the North Sea at Bremerhaven.

willibrord.s: Willibrord was an Anglo-Saxon missionary from Northumbria, known as the Apostle of the Frisians. Arriving in Frisia in 690 with the support of Pippin of Herstal, he was consecrated archbishop of the Frisians by Pope Sergius I in 695 and made Utrecht his see.

witwatersrand.s: The Witwatersrand is a low ridge and the surrounding region in Gauteng, South Africa, where the world's richest gold deposits were discovered in 1886. The gold rush created Johannesburg and transformed the South African Republic, drawing foreign miners whose grievances helped…

wilhelm-solf.s: Wilhelm Solf was a German colonial administrator and diplomat. As the first governor of German Samoa from 1900 to 1911, he ruled through Samoan chiefs, limited land sales and suppressed opposition such as the Mau a Pule.

wanggeom-seong.s: Wanggeom-seong was the capital of Gojoseon in its last centuries, usually located near modern Pyongyang on the Taedong river. Under Wiman and his grandson Ugeo it withstood a siege by the armies of Emperor Wu of Han for about a year before falling in 108 BCE, after which the…

wurzburg-residence.s: The Würzburg Residence is the baroque palace of the prince-bishops of Würzburg in Bavaria, Germany, built mainly between 1720 and 1744 to designs by Balthasar Neumann. Its grand staircase is covered by a vast ceiling fresco painted by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo in 1752–1753,…

wareru.s: Wareru was the founder of the Mon kingdom of Martaban, later called Hanthawaddy, in lower Burma. A Mon of humble origin, he seized Martaban in 1287 after the fall of the Pagan Kingdom and gained recognition from King Ram Khamhaeng of Sukhothai.

wat-phra-that-hariphunchai.s: Wat Phra That Hariphunchai is a Buddhist temple in Lamphun, northern Thailand, centred on a gilded stupa said to enshrine a relic of the Buddha. Tradition credits its founding to King Adityaraja of the Mon kingdom of Hariphunchai.

wyandot.s: The Wyandot are an Indigenous people formed in the 17th century from Wendat and Petun refugees after the Iroquois destroyed their homelands in 1649-1650. They settled around Detroit and in northern Ohio, where they became leading members of Indigenous alliances against…

walafrid-strabo.s: Walafrid Strabo was a Frankish monk, poet and theologian, educated at Reichenau and at Fulda under Rabanus Maurus. He served as tutor to the young Charles the Bald at the court of Louis the Pious and from 838 was abbot of Reichenau, on Lake Constance.

welf-i-duke-of-bavaria.s: Welf I, Duke of Bavaria, counted as Welf IV of his family, was the founder of the Bavarian line of the House of Welf. Made duke by Emperor Henry IV in 1070, he was deposed in 1077 for joining the emperor's opponents in the Investiture Controversy and restored in 1096.

werden.s: Werden is a district of Essen in the Ruhr, Germany, on the river Ruhr. It grew around Werden Abbey, founded around 799 by the Frisian missionary Saint Ludger, whose abbots ruled a small territory as princes of the Empire until 1803.

wiener-neustadt.s: Wiener Neustadt is a city in Lower Austria, south of Vienna, founded in 1194 by Duke Leopold V of Austria as a fortified frontier town against Hungary. Emperor Frederick III often resided in its castle in the 15th century, and he and his son Maximilian I are associated with it.

washington-dc.s: Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States, on the Potomac River between Maryland and Virginia. Planned on a site chosen by George Washington, it has been the seat of the federal government since 1800 and houses Congress, the White House and the Supreme Court.

walwal-incident.s: The Walwal incident was a clash on 5 December 1934 at the wells of Walwal in the Ogaden, between Ethiopian troops and the Italian colonial garrison, which had occupied the oasis inside Ethiopian territory. Italy demanded compensation and an apology, and the dispute, taken to…

windward-maroons.s: The Windward Maroons were the Maroon communities of eastern Jamaica, formed by Africans who escaped slavery and settled in the Blue Mountains and the John Crow Mountains. Led by figures such as Nanny and Quao, they resisted the British in the First Maroon War and made peace in…

wanyan-liang.s: Wanyan Liang was the fourth emperor of the Jurchen Jin dynasty, ruling from 1150 to 1161 after murdering his predecessor. He centralised power and moved the capital south to Zhongdu, modern Beijing, in 1153.

warangal.s: Warangal, historically Orugallu, is a city in Telangana, India, and was the capital of the Kakatiya dynasty from the late 12th century. Its fort, with great stone gateways, was taken by the Delhi Sultanate in 1323, recovered by the Musunuri Nayaks in the 1330s and later held…

william-moorcroft.s: William Moorcroft was an English veterinary surgeon and explorer who managed the East India Company's horse stud in Bengal. In search of horses he travelled through the western Himalaya, Ladakh and Kashmir, and from 1819 led a long expedition through Afghanistan towards Bukhara.

william-henry-scott.s: William Henry Scott was an American-born historian of the Philippines who lived and taught there for most of his life. His Prehispanic Source Materials for the Study of Philippine History (1968) exposed the Code of Kalantiaw as a forgery and treated the Maragtas as folklore.

william-ruto.s: William Ruto is a Kenyan politician who has been president of Kenya since 2022. He rose in KANU under Daniel arap Moi and served as deputy president under Uhuru Kenyatta from 2013 to 2022.

western-deffufa.s: The Western Deffufa is a massive mud-brick structure at Kerma in northern Sudan, the main temple of the Kerma kingdom. Built and enlarged over many centuries, it still stands about 18 metres high.

wakayama.s: Wakayama is a city on the west coast of the Kii Peninsula in Japan, at the mouth of the Kinokawa river, and the capital of Wakayama Prefecture. Toyotomi Hideyoshi had a castle built there in 1585, and from 1619 it was the seat of the Kii branch of the Tokugawa, one of the…

wakayama-prefecture.s: Wakayama Prefecture is a prefecture of Japan in the Kansai region, covering the western and southern part of the Kii Peninsula, with its capital at Wakayama. It was created in 1871 from the Kii domain when the domains were abolished.

wallonia.s: Wallonia is the mainly French-speaking southern region of Belgium, with its capital at Namur and major cities including Liège, Charleroi and Mons. Its coal, iron and glass industries made it the heart of Belgium's industrialisation in the 19th century, the first on the…

wuffa.s: Wuffa was the semi-legendary founder of the East Anglian royal house, from whom the dynasty took the name Wuffingas. Later genealogies make him the grandfather of Rædwald and place his rule in the 6th century, but nothing about him is securely known.

wuffingas.s: The Wuffingas were the ruling dynasty of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of East Anglia from the 6th century until about 749, named after their ancestor Wuffa. Its members included Rædwald, probably commemorated at Sutton Hoo, and King Anna, whose daughters founded monasteries at Ely…

west-yorkshire.s: West Yorkshire is a metropolitan county of northern England, created in 1974 and including Leeds, Bradford, Wakefield, Huddersfield and Halifax. It grew in the 18th and 19th centuries as the centre of the English wool textile industry.

westminster-vermont.s: Westminster is a town in south-eastern Vermont, on the Connecticut River. A convention held there in January 1777 declared the independence of the New Hampshire Grants as the state of New Connecticut, soon renamed Vermont.

william-fitzosbern.s: William FitzOsbern was a Norman lord, kinsman and close adviser of William the Conqueror, and one of the planners of the invasion of England in 1066. Made Earl of Hereford, he built castles at Chepstow and elsewhere to push Norman power into south-east Wales.

wadi-hadhramaut.s: Wadi Hadhramaut is a long valley system in eastern Yemen, running roughly parallel to the Arabian Sea coast. Watered by seasonal floods, its fields supported the ancient Kingdom of Hadramawt, and in later centuries towns such as Shibam, Seiyun and Tarim grew there, famous for…

walcheren.s: Walcheren is a former island in the Dutch province of Zeeland, at the mouth of the Scheldt, now joined to the mainland by reclaimed land. Its port of Vlissingen (Flushing) commanded the approach to Antwerp.

wihtred-of-kent.s: Wihtred was king of Kent from about 690 to 725, restoring stability after a period of invasion and disputed succession. His law code of 695 deals mainly with the Church, setting penalties for pagan worship, unlawful marriage and failure to keep the Sabbath, and he granted the…

wu-chen.s: Wu Chen was a rebel leader in the rising against the Qin dynasty. A follower of Chen Sheng, he was sent north to take the old lands of Zhao and in 209 BCE proclaimed himself king of Zhao, sending his general Han Guang to occupy Yan, where Han Guang made himself king instead.

wheelus-air-base.s: Wheelus Air Base was a United States Air Force base near Tripoli, Libya, used from 1943 until 1970. During the Cold War it was one of the largest American bases outside the United States, used for training and by Strategic Air Command, and its rent was an important source of…

woden.s: Woden was the chief god of the pagan Anglo-Saxons, corresponding to the Norse Odin and the continental Wodan. Associated with wisdom, war, poetry and the dead, he gave his name to Wednesday.

wilhelm-karl-duke-of-urach.s: Wilhelm Karl, Duke of Urach, was a German prince and general of a Catholic branch of the royal house of Württemberg. On 11 July 1918 the Council of Lithuania elected him king of Lithuania as Mindaugas II, hoping a monarchy would loosen German control.

waldrada.s: Waldrada was the mistress and, for a time, the wife of King Lothair II of Lotharingia, by whom she had a son, Hugh, and daughters. Lothair tried to repudiate his queen Teutberga and marry Waldrada, but Pope Nicholas I declared their marriage invalid and excommunicated her in 866.

wadjet.s: Wadjet was an ancient Egyptian cobra goddess, the protector of Lower Egypt, worshipped above all at Buto in the Nile Delta. Shown as a rearing cobra or as a woman wearing the red crown, she was paired with the vulture goddess Nekhbet of Upper Egypt in the king's 'Two Ladies'…

wadd.s: Wadd was the national god of the ancient Kingdom of Ma'in in Yemen, a moon god often associated with the snake. Minaean inscriptions call the people the children of Wadd, and his cult spread along the incense route.

wadiyar-dynasty.s: The Wodeyar or Wadiyar dynasty ruled Mysore in southern India, by tradition from 1399 until after Indian independence. Vassals of Vijayanagara at first, they became independent after Raja Wodeyar I took Srirangapatna in 1610.

woyo.s: The Woyo are a Kongo people living in the Cabinda enclave of Angola and the coastal area around the mouth of the Congo River. They formed the population of the kingdom of Ngoyo, which traded with Europeans at the port of Cabinda from the 17th to the 19th century.

whitby-abbey.s: Whitby Abbey was a monastery on the North Yorkshire coast founded in 657 by King Oswiu of Northumbria, with Abbess Hild ruling a double house of monks and nuns. In 664 it hosted the Synod of Whitby, at which Oswiu chose Roman over Irish practice for dating Easter.

william-wallace.s: William Wallace was a Scottish leader in the First War of Scottish Independence. With Andrew Murray he defeated an English army at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297 and was made Guardian of Scotland, but he was beaten by Edward I at Falkirk in 1298.

west-timor.s: West Timor is the western part of the island of Timor, forming part of the Indonesian province of East Nusa Tenggara, with its capital at Kupang. Its mountainous interior was divided among Atoni domains such as Sonbai and Amanuban, while the Dutch, based at Kupang from 1653,…

west-sussex.s: West Sussex is a county in south-east England on the English Channel, with Chichester as its county town. It became a separate administrative county in 1889, and together with East Sussex it covers the land of the old kingdom of the South Saxons.

wilfrid.s: Wilfrid was a Northumbrian bishop and saint who championed Roman church practice at the Synod of Whitby in 664 and became Bishop of York. Repeatedly expelled after quarrels with kings and archbishops, he appealed twice to Rome, and during one exile he converted the South…

warwickshire.s: Warwickshire is a county in the West Midlands of England, with Warwick as its county town. Its western part once lay in the kingdom of the Hwicce and the rest in Mercia.

worcester.s: Worcester is a cathedral city on the River Severn in the English West Midlands. A bishopric was founded there around 680 for the Hwicce, and the diocese long preserved the kingdom's outline.

worcester-v-georgia.s: Worcester v. Georgia was an 1832 case in which the United States Supreme Court, under Chief Justice John Marshall, overturned the conviction of the missionary Samuel Worcester for living in Cherokee territory without a Georgia licence.

wulfhere-of-mercia.s: Wulfhere was king of Mercia from 658 to 675, a son of Penda. He threw off Northumbrian rule and made Mercia the dominant power in southern England, controlling Surrey, London and Essex.

wilhelmina-of-the-netherlands.s: Wilhelmina was queen of the Netherlands from 1890 to 1948, under the regency of her mother Emma until 1898. When Germany invaded in May 1940 she escaped to London, where she headed the government in exile and became a symbol of resistance through her radio broadcasts.

willem-alexander-of-the-netherlands.s: Willem-Alexander is king of the Netherlands, who succeeded on 30 April 2013 when his mother Beatrix abdicated. He is the first male Dutch monarch since 1890, after three successive queens.

werra.s: The Werra is a river of about 300 kilometres in Thuringia and Hesse, central Germany. At Hann.

winterthur.s: Winterthur is a city in the Swiss canton of Zürich, north-east of the city of Zürich, and the canton's second largest town. In 919 Duke Burchard II of Swabia defeated King Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy near the town.

wallis-island.s: Wallis Island, called Uvea by its inhabitants, is the main island of the French overseas collectivity of Wallis and Futuna in the south-west Pacific. Surrounded by a lagoon and small islets, it holds the territory's capital, Mata-Utu.

wat-si-saket.s: Wat Si Saket is a Buddhist temple in Vientiane, Laos, built by King Anouvong in 1818. Its cloister walls hold thousands of small Buddha images in niches, together with several hundred seated statues.

wolaita-zone.s: Wolaita Zone is an administrative zone in southern Ethiopia, between the Omo river and Lake Abaya, with its capital at Wolaita Sodo. It covers the heartland of the former kingdom of Wolaita, conquered by Menelik II in 1894.

wiremu-tamihana.s: Wiremu Tāmihana was a chief of Ngāti Hauā in the Waikato, New Zealand, and a Christian who led his people in building a mission settlement. He was the leading organiser of the King movement, supporting the choice of Pōtatau Te Wherowhero as the first Māori King in 1858, and he…

welser-family.s: The Welser were a family of merchants and bankers of Augsburg, in southern Germany, among the richest in Europe in the 16th century alongside the Fuggers. They traded in spices, textiles and metals from Lisbon to Antwerp and lent large sums to Charles V.

white-movement.s: The White movement was the loose coalition of anti-Bolshevik forces in the Russian Civil War. Led mainly by former tsarist officers such as Kornilov, Denikin, Kolchak, Yudenich and Wrangel, and supported at times by the Allies and by Cossack hosts, its armies fought from the…

walther-von-der-vogelweide.s: Walther von der Vogelweide was the most celebrated German lyric poet of the Middle Ages. He wrote love songs in the Minnesang tradition as well as political poems commenting on the struggles between emperors and popes, and he served patrons including the Babenberg dukes of…

wartburg.s: The Wartburg is a castle on a hill above Eisenach in Thuringia, Germany, traditionally founded around 1067 by Louis the Bearded. It was the court of the Ludowingian landgraves, home of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary and the setting of the legendary contest of minstrels.

wolfram-von-eschenbach.s: Wolfram von Eschenbach was a German knight and poet, one of the greatest writers of medieval German literature. His epic Parzival, adapted from Chrétien de Troyes, tells the story of the knight's quest for the Grail; he also wrote the unfinished Willehalm and Titurel.

wat-chet-yot.s: Wat Chet Yot is a Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai, Thailand, founded by King Tilokarat of Lan Na in 1455. Its main building, with seven spires, was modelled on the Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha attained enlightenment.

warad-sin.s: Warad-Sin was king of Larsa in southern Mesopotamia, installed by his father Kudur-Mabuk, an Amorite chief. During his reign he carried out extensive building works at Ur, Larsa and other cities, and his father continued to exercise strong influence.

wassaf.s: Wassaf, Abdallah ibn Fadlallah of Shiraz, was a Persian historian and official of the Ilkhanate. His Tarikh-i Wassaf, a continuation of Juvayni's history of the Mongols, covers the Ilkhanate and neighbouring lands from 1257 to the 1320s in a highly ornate style.

waffen-ss.s: The Waffen-SS was the armed wing of the Nazi SS, which grew from a few regiments into an army of some 38 divisions during the Second World War. It took in volunteers and conscripts from occupied and allied countries, including Latvian and Estonian legions.

wat-phra-si-rattana-mahathat-lopburi.s: Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat is a ruined temple near the railway station of Lopburi in central Thailand. Its central tower was built in the Khmer style, probably in the 12th or 13th century, and later additions date from the Ayutthaya period, when King Narai lived at Lopburi.

wen-xuan.s: The Wen Xuan (Selections of Refined Literature) is an anthology of Chinese poetry and prose compiled in the early 6th century under Xiao Tong, crown prince of the Liang dynasty. Its 30 chapters, later divided into 60, gather some 700 works by about 130 writers from the Zhou to…

wenno.s: Wenno was the first master of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, the crusading order founded in 1202 to conquer and convert Livonia. He led its early campaigns against the Livs and Latgalians from Riga.

william-fraser-delhi.s: William Fraser was a Scottish official of the East India Company, soldier, administrator and collector of Indian art, who served at Delhi as commissioner and agent to the governor-general. A Persian scholar who lived much like a Mughal nobleman, he was shot dead in Delhi in…

walter-devereux-1st-earl-of-essex.s: Walter Devereux, 1st Earl of Essex, was an English nobleman who in 1573 led a private venture, backed by Elizabeth I, to colonise Clandeboye in Ulster. The enterprise was marked by brutality, including the seizure and execution of Sir Brian MacPhelim O'Neill in 1574 and the…

whithorn.s: Whithorn is a small town in Galloway, south-west Scotland, associated with Saint Ninian, who according to Bede founded a stone church there called Candida Casa, the 'White House'. It was a Northumbrian bishopric in the 8th century, and the see was revived in the 12th century…

welshry.s: The Welshry was the part of a Marcher lordship in medieval Wales where native Welsh tenants lived under Welsh law and custom, as opposed to the Englishry, where settlers held land under English law. The division, usually between an upland Welshry and a lowland Englishry,…

wangerland.s: Wangerland is a coastal district in Friesland in north-western Germany, north of Jever. In the Middle Ages it was one of the free Frisian lands, governed by its own peasant communities before chieftains took power in the 14th century, and it later formed part of the Lordship…

white-elster.s: The White Elster is a river in central Germany, about 250 kilometres long, a tributary of the Saale. It rises in the Czech Republic near Aš and flows through the Vogtland past Plauen, Greiz and Gera to Leipzig, joining the Saale near Halle.

weida.s: Weida is a small town in eastern Thuringia, Germany, on the river Weida. Its Osterburg castle was the seat of the advocates (Vögte) of Weida, imperial officials who governed the region for the Hohenstaufen emperors and gave the Vogtland its name.

waren-muritz.s: Waren is a town in Mecklenburg, north-eastern Germany, on the northern shore of the Müritz, the largest lake lying wholly within Germany. Founded in the 13th century, it belonged to the lords of Werle, who had a residence there, and later to Mecklenburg.

waldenburg-saxony.s: Waldenburg is a small town on the Zwickauer Mulde in western Saxony, Germany. Acquired by the Schönburg family in the 14th century, it became the residence of their Schönburg-Waldenburg line, whose castle was rebuilt as a palace in the 19th century.

william-hicks.s: William Hicks, known as Hicks Pasha, was a British army officer who commanded the Egyptian forces in Sudan against the Mahdist uprising. In 1883 he led an army of several thousand men into Kordofan, where the Mahdi's Ansar annihilated it at Shaykan, near El Obeid, in November.

wexford.s: Wexford is a port town in south-eastern Ireland at the mouth of the River Slaney. It grew from a Norse settlement of the 9th or 10th century, and in 1169 it became the first town in Ireland captured by the Anglo-Normans, who had been invited by Diarmait Mac Murchada, King of…

warta.s: The Warta is a river in western and central Poland, about 800 kilometres long and the longest tributary of the Oder. It flows past Sieradz, Poznań and Gorzów Wielkopolski and joins the Oder at Kostrzyn.

william-fitzwilliam-owen.s: William Fitzwilliam Owen was a British naval officer and hydrographer who surveyed much of the coast of East and West Africa in the 1820s. At Mombasa in 1824 he accepted the Mazrui rulers' request for protection against the Busaidi of Oman and declared a British protectorate…

wang-chao.s: Wang Chao was a Chinese warlord of the late Tang dynasty who founded Wang family rule in Fujian. A leader of a band of soldiers from Henan, he took Fuzhou in 893 with his brothers and was recognised by the Tang court as military governor of the region.

wang-yanzheng.s: Wang Yanzheng was the last ruler of the Min kingdom in Fujian during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. A son of Wang Shenzhi, he rebelled against his brother, the emperor Wang Yanxi, and in 943 proclaimed his own state, Yin, at Jianzhou.

william-johnson.s: Sir William Johnson was an Irish-born colonial official in New York who became British superintendent of Indian affairs for the northern colonies in 1756. Settled in the Mohawk valley, he learned the Mohawk language, took Molly Brant as his consort and built close ties with…

waghji-ii.s: Waghji II was the Thakore Sahib of Morvi, a princely state in Kathiawar, western India, from 1870 to 1922. Educated at the Rajkumar College in Rajkot, he modernised his state, building the Morvi Railway, a tramway and the port of Navlakhi, and promoting trade and local industry.

war-of-jenkins-ear.s: The War of Jenkins' Ear was a conflict between Great Britain and Spain fought mainly in the Caribbean and on the American mainland from 1739. It took its name from the ear of Robert Jenkins, a British captain mutilated by Spanish coastguards in 1731.

wat-phra-mahathat-woramahawihan.s: Wat Phra Mahathat Woramahawihan is the chief Buddhist temple of Nakhon Si Thammarat in southern Thailand. Its great white stupa, the Phra Borommathat Chedi, built in Sri Lankan style, is believed to enshrine relics of the Buddha and became one of the most revered pilgrimage…

wat-phumin.s: Wat Phumin is a Buddhist temple in the city of Nan in northern Thailand, founded in 1596 and restored in the 19th century. Its cruciform hall, with four entrances guarded by great serpents, houses four Buddha images facing the cardinal directions.

wehrmacht.s: The Wehrmacht was the unified armed forces of Nazi Germany from 1935 to 1945, comprising the army, navy and air force. Built up rapidly in defiance of the Treaty of Versailles, it won swift victories early in the Second World War before being worn down on the Eastern Front and…

william-goffe.s: William Goffe was an English Parliamentarian officer and one of the judges who signed the death warrant of Charles I in 1649, later a major-general under Oliver Cromwell. At the Restoration in 1660 he fled to New England with his father-in-law Edward Whalley.

willem-kieft.s: Willem Kieft was Director of New Netherland from 1638 to 1647. His attempt to tax the Lenape and other local peoples, and the massacres at Pavonia and Corlears Hook in 1643, provoked Kieft's War of 1643 to 1645, which devastated the colony.

waitangi-tribunal.s: The Waitangi Tribunal is a permanent commission of inquiry in New Zealand, set up by the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 to investigate claims by Māori that the Crown has breached the promises of the Treaty of Waitangi. From 1985 it could hear claims reaching back to 1840.

white-sea.s: The White Sea is an inlet of the Barents Sea on the north-western coast of Russia, enclosed by the Kola Peninsula and Karelia. Its coasts formed part of Novgorod's northern lands and were settled by Pomors.

wagri.s: The Wagri, or Wagrians, were a West Slavic tribe who lived in eastern Holstein, a region still called Wagria, from about the 8th to the 12th century. Part of the Obotrite confederation, they had their chief stronghold at Starigard (Oldenburg in Holstein).

wisconsin.s: Wisconsin is a state of the upper Midwest of the United States, between Lake Michigan and Lake Superior, with its capital at Madison. Explored by the French from the 17th century, it passed to Britain and then to the United States, and became a state in 1848.

wales.s: Wales is a country of the United Kingdom on the western side of Great Britain, with its capital at Cardiff. After Roman rule it was divided among Welsh kingdoms such as Gwynedd, Powys and Deheubarth, until Edward I of England conquered the last native principality in…

walvis-bay.s: Walvis Bay is a port town on the Atlantic coast of Namibia, the only good natural harbour on that desert shore. In the 19th century it was the outlet for the cattle, ivory and gun trade of the interior, and Britain annexed the bay in 1878, later attaching it to the Cape Colony.

windhoek.s: Windhoek is the capital and largest city of Namibia, in the central highlands. Jonker Afrikaner settled there around 1840 and made it the base of the Oorlam Afrikaners, but it was abandoned in the 1860s.

west-galicia.s: West Galicia was the name of the Polish lands, including Kraków, Lublin and Radom, that Austria annexed in the Third Partition of Poland in 1795. Austria lost the province by the Treaty of Schönbrunn in 1809 to the Duchy of Warsaw, regaining only the Kraków region later, in 1846.

wat-chaiwatthanaram.s: Wat Chaiwatthanaram is a Buddhist temple on the Chao Phraya river just outside the island of Ayutthaya, built from 1630 by King Prasat Thong. Its central prang and surrounding towers, modelled on Khmer temple plans, represent Mount Meru and the Buddhist cosmos.

wat-phra-si-sanphet.s: Wat Phra Si Sanphet was the royal temple within the palace grounds of Ayutthaya, used for royal ceremonies and without resident monks. Founded in the fifteenth century, it is known for three great bell-shaped chedis that held the ashes of kings.

wa-japan.s: Wa was the name used in Chinese and Korean sources for the people and polities of the Japanese archipelago from the first centuries CE. Chinese histories describe Wa rulers such as Himiko sending embassies, and Korean sources record Wa as allies of Baekje and enemies of Silla…

wars-of-the-roses.s: The Wars of the Roses were a series of civil wars for the English throne between the houses of Lancaster and York, branches of the Plantagenet dynasty, from 1455 to 1487. Weak rule under Henry VI led to rival claims, and the crown changed hands several times.

war-measures-act.s: The War Measures Act was a Canadian law of 1914 that gave the federal government emergency powers to rule by decree in times of war, invasion or insurrection. It was used in both world wars, including for the internment of Ukrainian and Japanese Canadians, and in peacetime…

wilfrid-laurier.s: Wilfrid Laurier was a Liberal prime minister of Canada from 1896 to 1911, the first French Canadian to hold the office. His government promoted mass immigration that settled the prairies, created the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905 and sought compromise between…

wadenswil.s: Wädenswil is a town on the south-western shore of Lake Zürich in the canton of Zürich, Switzerland. It belonged to the Knights Hospitaller until Zürich acquired it in the mid-sixteenth century and made it a bailiwick.

war-of-the-second-coalition.s: The War of the Second Coalition was fought between Revolutionary France and an alliance of Britain, Austria, Russia, the Ottoman Empire and others. After early coalition successes in Italy and Switzerland in 1799, including the battles around Zürich, France under Napoleon…

western-ganga-dynasty.s: The Western Ganga dynasty ruled southern Karnataka in India from about 350 to 1000, with capitals at Kolar and later Talakad. Often subordinate allies of the Chalukyas of Badami and then of the Rashtrakutas, they were major patrons of Jainism; the colossal statue of…

walter-burley-griffin.s: Walter Burley Griffin was an American architect of the Prairie School who, with his wife Marion Mahony Griffin, won the international competition of 1912 to design Australia's new capital, Canberra. He directed the city's early construction until 1920, though his plan was only…

william-sheppard.s: William Sheppard was an African American Presbyterian missionary in the Kasai region of the Congo Free State from 1890, known for his work among the Kuba. In 1899 he documented killings by state-backed raiders hunting for rubber and published his findings, and in 1909 he was…

william-stairs.s: William Stairs was a Canadian-born British army officer and explorer. After serving on Henry Morton Stanley's Emin Pasha Relief Expedition, he led an expedition for King Leopold II's Congo Free State to Katanga in 1891–1892, racing the British South Africa Company.

william-clito.s: William Clito was the son of Robert Curthose, duke of Normandy, and a claimant to Normandy against his uncle Henry I of England. After the murder of Charles the Good in 1127, King Louis VI of France imposed him as count of Flanders, but his demands soon turned the towns…

walloon-flanders.s: Walloon Flanders was the French-speaking southern part of the County of Flanders, made up of the castellanies of Lille, Douai and Orchies. Held by the French crown from 1312 to 1369, it returned to Flanders with the Burgundian marriage and joined the Union of Arras in 1579.

war-of-the-two-peters.s: The War of the Two Peters was fought between Peter I of Castile and Peter IV of Aragon from 1356. Castilian armies repeatedly invaded Aragon and Valencia, and the conflict merged with the Castilian civil war, in which Aragon backed Henry of Trastámara.

warsaw-pact.s: The Warsaw Pact was the military alliance of the Soviet Union and the communist states of Eastern Europe, signed in Warsaw on 14 May 1955 after West Germany joined NATO. Its forces were used against members, as in the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.

walderada.s: Walderada was a Lombard princess of the sixth century, daughter of King Wacho. She married the Frankish king Theudebald of Austrasia and, after his death in 555, his great-uncle Chlothar I, who gave her up because the Church condemned the marriage.

william-of-ockham.s: William of Ockham was an English Franciscan friar and philosopher, one of the leading thinkers of late medieval scholasticism. Summoned to Avignon over his teachings, he sided with his order's leaders against Pope John XXII in the dispute over apostolic poverty and fled in…

walloon-brabant.s: Walloon Brabant is a province of Belgium in the Walloon Region, created in 1995 when the old province of Brabant was divided. Its capital is Wavre, and its towns include Nivelles, Waterloo and Louvain-la-Neuve, home of the French-speaking UCLouvain.

war-of-the-limburg-succession.s: The War of the Limburg Succession was fought from 1283 to 1289 over the Duchy of Limburg after the death of Duchess Ermengard in 1283. Duke John I of Brabant, who had bought the claim of her kinsman Adolf of Berg, faced Count Reinald I of Guelders, Ermengard's widower, backed…

wenceslaus-i-duke-of-luxembourg.s: Wenceslaus I was duke of Luxembourg and, through his marriage to Duchess Joanna, duke of Brabant and Limburg from 1355 until his death in 1383. A son of John the Blind of Bohemia and half-brother of Emperor Charles IV, he swore the Joyous Entry with Joanna in 1356.

well-of-moses.s: The Well of Moses is a monumental sculpture by Claus Sluter and his workshop, made in 1395–1405 for the cloister of the Charterhouse of Champmol near Dijon. Its hexagonal base, carved with six life-size Old Testament prophets led by Moses, once supported a Calvary group, of…

westminster-abbey.s: Westminster Abbey is a church in Westminster, London, rebuilt by Edward the Confessor and consecrated in 1065, then rebuilt again in Gothic style from 1245 under Henry III. Every English and British monarch since William the Conqueror, crowned there on Christmas Day 1066, has…

william-adelin.s: William Adelin was the only legitimate son of Henry I of England and Matilda of Scotland, and heir to England and Normandy. He received the homage of the Norman barons and in 1120 did homage to Louis VI of France for the duchy.

william-longsword.s: William Longsword was the son of Rollo and ruler of Normandy from about 927 to 942. In 933 King Rudolph of West Francia granted him further lands in the west, probably the Cotentin and the Avranchin, giving Normandy roughly its later borders.

william-of-jumieges.s: William of Jumièges was a monk of the Norman abbey of Jumièges and the author of the Gesta Normannorum ducum, a history of the dukes of Normandy. Building on the work of Dudo of Saint-Quentin, he continued the story to the conquest of England and presented it to William the…

william-of-volpiano.s: William of Volpiano was an Italian-born Benedictine monk, abbot of Saint-Bénigne in Dijon and a leading figure of the Cluniac reform. Invited by Duke Richard II, he reformed the abbey of Fécamp in Normandy from 1001 and spread monastic reform to many Norman houses, laying the…

william-ii-of-england.s: William II, called Rufus, was the third son of William the Conqueror and king of England from 1087. He put down rebellions by barons who favoured his elder brother Robert Curthose, and in 1096 took Normandy in pledge from Robert, who was leaving on the First Crusade.

war-of-parma.s: The War of Parma was fought in 1551–1552 between Pope Julius III and Emperor Charles V on one side and Ottavio Farnese, duke of Parma, backed by Henry II of France, on the other. It began when Ottavio, fearing the loss of Parma, placed himself under French protection.

wartislaw-iii-duke-of-pomerania.s: Wartislaw III was duke of Pomerania-Demmin, of the Griffin dynasty, ruling alongside his cousin Barnim I. He promoted German settlement and granted town rights, including Lübeck law to Greifswald in 1250.

wartislaw-ix-duke-of-pomerania.s: Wartislaw IX was duke of Pomerania-Wolgast, of the Griffin dynasty, from the 1410s until his death in 1457. He supported the founding of the University of Greifswald in 1456 by the burgomaster Heinrich Rubenow, one of the oldest universities of northern Europe.

wendish-crusade.s: The Wendish Crusade of 1147 was a campaign of Saxon, Danish and Polish princes against the pagan Slavs, or Wends, east of the Elbe, authorised by Pope Eugenius III as part of the Second Crusade. Armies led by Henry the Lion, Albert the Bear and others besieged Dobin and Demmin…

werla.s: Werla was a royal palace (Pfalz) of the Ottonian kings on the Oker river near Schladen in Lower Saxony. Henry the Fowler took refuge there from a Magyar raid in 926 before agreeing a nine-year truce, and Otto I and his successors held assemblies there.

william-v-prince-of-orange.s: William V, Prince of Orange, was the last stadtholder of the Dutch Republic, holding the office from 1751, as a child, until 1795. His weak rule and the defeats of the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War fed the Patriot movement, which challenged his powers until a Prussian invasion…

western-new-guinea.s: Western New Guinea is the western half of the island of New Guinea, administered by Indonesia since 1963 and now divided into several Papuan provinces. Ruled by the Netherlands as part of the East Indies and, from 1949 to 1962, as Netherlands New Guinea, it passed to Indonesia…

way-of-the-five-pecks-of-rice.n: Way of the Five Pecks of Rice
way-of-the-five-pecks-of-rice.s: The Way of the Five Pecks of Rice was an early Daoist religious movement founded in Sichuan in the second century CE by Zhang Daoling, named after the contribution of rice paid by its members. Under his grandson Zhang Lu it ran a theocratic state in Hanzhong until 215.

wang-dun.s: Wang Dun was a general of the Eastern Jin dynasty from the Wang clan of Langya and a cousin of the minister Wang Dao. As governor of Jing province on the middle Yangtze he commanded the strongest army of the new dynasty.

wang-clan-of-langya.s: The Wang clan of Langya was one of the most powerful aristocratic families of medieval China, originating in Langya commandery in Shandong. Its members Wang Dao and Wang Dun helped Sima Rui found the Eastern Jin dynasty, and contemporaries said that 'the Wang and the Sima…

wandsbek.s: Wandsbek is a borough in the north-east of Hamburg. A Holstein estate and town under Danish rule and later Prussian, it was known in the 18th century as the home of the poet Matthias Claudius, who published the newspaper Der Wandsbecker Bote there.

west-germany.s: West Germany was the common English name for the Federal Republic of Germany between its foundation in 1949 and German reunification in 1990. Formed from the American, British and French occupation zones with Bonn as its capital, it became a parliamentary democracy and a…

weser-renaissance.s: Weser Renaissance is the style of Renaissance architecture in the Weser region of north-western Germany, flourishing from about 1520 to 1620. Drawing on Dutch and Flemish models, it is marked by richly decorated gables, bay windows and bands of carved ornament.

willehad.s: Willehad (c. 745–789) was an Anglo-Saxon missionary from Northumbria who worked among the Frisians and Saxons.

wilhelm-kaisen.s: Wilhelm Kaisen (1887–1979) was a German Social Democratic politician who was mayor of Bremen and president of its senate from 1945 to 1965. He led the city's reconstruction after the Second World War and its re-establishment as a federal state in 1947.

warnier-law.s: The Warnier Law of July 1873, named after the deputy Auguste Warnier, extended French property law to land in Algeria. By breaking up collectively held tribal and family land into individual titles that could be sold, it allowed European settlers and speculators to acquire…

william-merlaud-ponty.s: William Merlaud-Ponty was a French colonial administrator who served as governor-general of French West Africa from 1908 until his death in 1915. He completed the conquest of the interior, abolished some forms of domestic slavery, and pursued a policy that favoured local…

wartburg-festival.s: The Wartburg Festival was a gathering of about 500 German students at the Wartburg castle near Eisenach on 18 October 1817, marking the 300th anniversary of Luther's Reformation and the fourth anniversary of the Battle of Leipzig. Students called for national unity and burned…

wunu-mountain.s: Wunü Mountain is a flat-topped mountain near Huanren in Liaoning province, China, crowned by a stone-walled fortress of the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo. It is usually identified with Jolbon, the first capital founded according to tradition by Jumong in 37 BCE.

wihwa-island.s: Wihwa Island is an island in the Yalu River near modern Sinuiju, on the border between North Korea and China. In 1388 the Goryeo general Yi Seong-gye, sent to attack Ming forces in Liaodong, halted there and turned his army back to the capital.

woyzeck.s: Woyzeck is an unfinished play by Georg Büchner, written in 1836-1837 and left in fragments at his death. It tells of a poor soldier, exploited and humiliated, who murders the woman he loves.

werner-report.s: The Werner Report was a plan for economic and monetary union in the European Communities, presented in October 1970 by a group chaired by Pierre Werner, prime minister of Luxembourg. It proposed reaching full union in stages within ten years, with fixed exchange rates, free…

wolfgang-amadeus-mozart.s: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a composer born in Salzburg who settled in Vienna in 1781 and became one of the greatest figures of the Viennese Classical style. A child prodigy who toured Europe, he wrote over 600 works, including the operas The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni…

western-chalukya-empire.s: The Western Chalukya Empire was a dynasty that ruled much of the western Deccan of India from 973 to 1189, founded by Tailapa II after the fall of the Rashtrakutas and governing from Kalyani. It fought long wars with the Cholas, and under Vikramaditya VI it reached its height.

wang-chongyang.s: Wang Chongyang, born Wang Zhe, was a Daoist teacher of the Jin dynasty from Shaanxi and the founder of the Quanzhen (Complete Perfection) School. After failing in an official career, he said he had met immortals in 1159 and lived for years as a hermit.

wanyan-chenglin.s: Wanyan Chenglin was the last emperor of the Jurchen Jin dynasty. In February 1234, as Mongol and Song armies stormed the city of Caizhou, the emperor Aizong abdicated in his favour and took his own life.

wanyan-xiyin.s: Wanyan Xiyin was a Jurchen noble and minister of the Jin dynasty, a kinsman of its founder Aguda. At Aguda's command he created the Jurchen script in 1119, combining elements of Chinese characters and the Khitan scripts, which was used for government documents and translations…

wanyan-yongji.s: Wanyan Yongji, known by his posthumous title Weishao Wang (Prince of Weishao), was emperor of the Jurchen Jin dynasty from 1208 to 1213. A son of the emperor Shizong, he faced the first great Mongol invasion under Genghis Khan, whose victory at Yehuling in 1211 exposed the…

west-baray.s: The West Baray is a huge rectangular reservoir at Angkor in Cambodia, about 8 kilometres long and over 2 kilometres wide, built in the eleventh century. On an island at its centre stands the West Mebon temple.

wamara.s: Wamara is remembered in the traditions of the Great Lakes region of East Africa as the last ruler of the Bachwezi, the semi-legendary dynasty of the kingdom of Kitara. Nkore tradition makes his son Ruhinda the founder of its Hinda dynasty, and Wamara is also venerated as one…

walhalla.s: Walhalla is a hall of fame in the form of a Greek Doric temple, built for King Ludwig I of Bavaria on a hill above the Danube near Regensburg. Designed by Leo von Klenze and built between 1830 and 1842, it holds busts and plaques honouring prominent figures of German-speaking…

wassily-kandinsky.s: Wassily Kandinsky was a Russian-born painter and art theorist, one of the pioneers of abstract art. Settling in Munich in 1896, he founded the Blue Rider group with Franz Marc in 1911 and set out his ideas in "Concerning the Spiritual in Art".

william-caxton.s: William Caxton was an English merchant, translator and printer who introduced printing to England. After learning the trade in Cologne and Bruges, where he printed the first book in English, he set up a press at Westminster in 1476.

william-shakespeare.s: William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet and actor, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language. Born in Stratford-upon-Avon, he worked in London with the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later the King's Men, and wrote about 39 plays, including Hamlet,…

william-pitt-the-younger.s: William Pitt the Younger was Prime Minister of Great Britain from 1783 to 1801 and again from 1804 to 1806, taking office at the age of 24. Son of William Pitt the Elder, he restored the public finances after the American war, introduced income tax and led Britain against…

william-pitt-the-elder.s: William Pitt the Elder, later 1st Earl of Chatham, was a British statesman who led the government during the Seven Years' War. From 1757 he concentrated British strength on naval power and colonial conquest while subsidising Prussia in Europe, and the 'year of victories' of…

william-wilberforce.s: William Wilberforce was an English politician and evangelical Christian who led the parliamentary campaign against the slave trade. Member of Parliament for Hull and later Yorkshire, he introduced abolition bills from 1789 until the Slave Trade Act was passed in 1807.

walloons.s: The Walloons are the French-speaking people of southern Belgium, named after the region of Wallonia. From the twelfth century groups of Walloons, together with Flemings and Germans, settled as privileged 'guests' in the Kingdom of Hungary, especially in and around towns such…

wenceslaus-iii-of-bohemia.s: Wenceslaus III was king of Hungary from 1301 to 1305, as Ladislaus V, and king of Bohemia and Poland in 1305–1306. Son of Wenceslaus II, he was elected in Hungary after the extinction of the Árpád dynasty but lost ground to Charles Robert of Anjou and handed his claim to Otto…

wladyslaw-iii-of-poland.s: Władysław III was king of Poland from 1434 and, as Vladislaus I, king of Hungary from 1440 until his death. His election in Hungary against the infant Ladislaus V led to civil war, but with John Hunyadi he waged the Long Campaign against the Ottomans in 1443–1444.

wide-streets-commission.s: The Wide Streets Commission was a body set up by the Irish Parliament in 1757 to lay out a broad new street from Essex Bridge to Dublin Castle. Over the following decades it planned much of Georgian Dublin, including Parliament Street, Westmoreland Street and D'Olier Street…

woollen-act.s: The Woollen Act was a law passed by the English Parliament in 1699 that banned the export of woollen cloth from Ireland to any country except England, where high duties already applied, in order to protect English manufacturers. It damaged the Irish woollen trade and…

war-of-saint-sabas.s: The War of Saint Sabas was a conflict between the Italian maritime republics of Genoa and Venice, fought mainly in and around Acre from 1256 to 1258, with fighting elsewhere until 1270. It began over property belonging to the monastery of Saint Sabas and drew the barons and…

waerferth-of-worcester.s: Wærferth was Bishop of Worcester from about 872 to 915, one of four Mercian scholars whom Alfred the Great brought to his court to revive learning. At Alfred's request he translated Pope Gregory the Great's Dialogues into Old English.

wiglaf-of-mercia.s: Wiglaf was king of Mercia from 827 to 829 and again from 830 to about 839. In 829 Ecgberht of Wessex drove him out and briefly ruled Mercia, but he recovered the kingdom the following year.

wulfred.s: Wulfred was Archbishop of Canterbury from 805 to 832. A reformer, he required the clergy of his cathedral to live a common life and sought to bring monasteries under episcopal control.

william-baillie.s: William Baillie (died 1782) was a Scottish officer of the British East India Company's Madras army. In September 1780, at the start of the Second Anglo-Mysore War, his detachment was surrounded and destroyed by Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan at Pollilur, one of the Company's…

welsh-marches.s: The Welsh Marches are the borderlands between England and Wales. After 1066 Norman lords seized much of eastern and southern Wales and ruled it as marcher lordships with their own courts and laws, outside the normal English shires.

wilhelm-von-humboldt.s: Wilhelm von Humboldt was a Prussian philosopher, linguist and statesman, elder brother of the naturalist Alexander von Humboldt. As head of education in the Prussian interior ministry in 1809–1810 he reformed schooling and founded the University of Berlin on the principle of…

wadi-dhana.s: Wadi Dhana (Adhanah) is a seasonal river valley in Yemen that carries floods from the western highlands down to the desert edge at Marib. The Sabaeans diverted its floods into channels that watered two great oases, works enlarged over many centuries into the Marib Dam.

william-dunbar.s: William Dunbar was a Scottish poet at the court of James IV, the most accomplished of the makars writing in Scots. His varied output includes The Thrissil and the Rois, celebrating the king's marriage to Margaret Tudor in 1503, comic and satirical verse and the Lament for the…

william-the-lion.s: William the Lion was King of Scots from 1165 to 1214, one of the longest reigns in Scottish history. Trying to recover Northumberland, he invaded England and was captured at Alnwick in 1174, and by the Treaty of Falaise he had to accept Henry II as his overlord until Richard I…

wassenaar-agreement.s: The Wassenaar Agreement was concluded on 24 November 1982 between Dutch employers' organisations and trade unions, at a time of high unemployment. Unions accepted wage moderation in return for shorter working hours and efforts to create jobs.

willem-drees.s: Willem Drees was a Dutch Labour politician who served as Prime Minister of the Netherlands from 1948 to 1958, leading coalitions of social democrats and Catholics. His governments rebuilt the country after the Second World War, oversaw the end of Dutch rule in Indonesia and…

wim-kok.s: Wim Kok was a Dutch trade union leader and Labour politician who served as Prime Minister of the Netherlands from 1994 to 2002. A co-architect of the Wassenaar Agreement as union leader, he led two 'purple' coalitions of social democrats and liberals, without the Christian…

wallingford.s: Wallingford is a market town on the River Thames in Oxfordshire, historically in Berkshire. Founded as one of Alfred the Great's burhs, with a planned street grid and earthen ramparts that still survive, it guarded an important river crossing.

wareham.s: Wareham is a market town in Dorset, southern England, between the rivers Frome and Piddle. A Saxon settlement with a minster church, it was occupied by the Danish army in 876 and later fortified as one of Alfred the Great's burhs, and its earthen ramparts are among the best…

wilhelm-maybach.s: Wilhelm Maybach was a German engineer from Heilbronn who, with Gottlieb Daimler, developed light, fast-running petrol engines at Cannstatt from the 1880s. He designed the first Mercedes car of 1901 for the Daimler company, and later founded his own firm, which built engines…

wat-chedi-luang.s: Wat Chedi Luang is a Buddhist temple in the centre of Chiang Mai, Thailand, whose great chedi was begun in the late 14th century and enlarged under King Tilokarat in the 15th, when it was the tallest structure in Lan Na. It housed the Emerald Buddha from 1468 to 1551.

wat-phra-singh.s: Wat Phra Singh is a Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai, Thailand, founded in 1345 by King Phayu of Lan Na to hold the ashes of his father. It houses the revered Phra Buddha Sihing image, and its Viharn Lai Kham, with murals of northern Thai life, is a classic example of Lan Na…

wat-suan-dok.s: Wat Suan Dok is a Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai, Thailand, built around 1371 by King Kue Na in his flower garden for the monk Sumana, who founded there a monastic lineage derived from Sri Lanka. Its great bell-shaped chedi is said to hold a relic of the Buddha, and white…

wisutthithewi.s: Wisutthithewi was the ruling queen of Lan Na from 1564 to 1578, a member of the old royal line of Mangrai who governed Chiang Mai as a vassal of the Burmese king Bayinnaung. After her death the Burmese appointed Bayinnaung's son Nawrahta Minsaw, ending native rule in Chiang…

wang-tong-ming-general.s: Wang Tong was a Ming general sent in 1426 to suppress Lê Lợi's rising in Vietnam. Defeated and besieged in Đông Quan, the Ming seat at modern Hanoi, he agreed after the destruction of the Ming relief army in 1427 to withdraw his forces to China, for which he was condemned at…

western-african-ebola-epidemic.s: The Western African Ebola epidemic was the largest outbreak of Ebola virus disease on record, spreading from Guinea in late 2013 to Liberia and Sierra Leone. It caused more than 28,000 cases and over 11,000 deaths, nearly 5,000 of them in Liberia, closing schools and halting…

william-tolbert.s: William Tolbert was the 20th president of Liberia, serving from 1971, when he succeeded William Tubman, until 1980. Leader of the True Whig Party, he faced growing opposition, and a proposed rise in the price of rice led to deadly riots in Monrovia in April 1979.

wadi-abu-dom.s: Wadi Abu Dom is a seasonal river valley in the Bayuda Desert of northern Sudan that joins the Nile near Merowe. It holds the ruins of the monastery of Ghazali, founded in the late 7th century in the kingdom of Makuria and one of the best-preserved monasteries of Christian Nubia.

waldemar-margrave-of-brandenburg.s: Waldemar the Great was Margrave of Brandenburg from 1308 to 1319, the last important ruler of the Ascanian line. He brought the whole Mark under his rule and defended it against a coalition of Denmark, Mecklenburg and other northern neighbours.

wadi-el-hudi.s: Wadi el-Hudi is a desert valley south-east of Aswan in Egypt and was the main source of amethyst in the Middle Kingdom. Expeditions from the Eleventh Dynasty onwards built camps and fortified settlements there and left many inscriptions recording their work.

white-chapel.s: The White Chapel is a limestone shrine built by Senusret I at Karnak for his jubilee festival, to hold the barque of the god Amun. Dismantled in the New Kingdom, its blocks were used as fill in the Third Pylon of Amenhotep III.

wang-yangming.s: Wang Yangming was a Chinese philosopher, official and general of the Ming dynasty, the most influential Neo-Confucian thinker after Zhu Xi. He taught that moral principle is found in one's own mind and that knowledge and action form a unity, and his School of Mind spread…

wanli-emperor.s: The Wanli Emperor was the 14th emperor of the Ming dynasty, reigning from 1572 to 1620, the longest reign of the dynasty. His early years saw the reforms of Zhang Juzheng and costly wars, including the defence of Korea against the Japanese invasions of the 1590s.

william-of-rubruck.s: William of Rubruck was a Flemish Franciscan friar who travelled to the Mongol Empire in 1253–1255 on behalf of King Louis IX of France. He reached the court of the Great Khan Möngke at Karakorum, where he took part in a religious debate, and wrote a detailed report on Mongol…

win-myint.s: Win Myint is a Myanmar politician of the National League for Democracy who was president from March 2018 until the military coup of 1 February 2021. A lawyer and former political prisoner, he had served as speaker of the lower house of parliament.

wannsee-conference.s: The Wannsee Conference was a meeting of senior Nazi officials held at a villa on the Wannsee lake in Berlin on 20 January 1942. Chaired by Reinhard Heydrich, it coordinated the government ministries and SS offices involved in the 'Final Solution', the deportation and murder of…

waikato-tainui.s: Waikato-Tainui is a confederation of Māori iwi of the Waikato region of New Zealand's North Island, descended from those who arrived on the Tainui canoe. It led the Kīngitanga, the Māori King Movement, from 1858, and lost much of its land in confiscations after the invasion of…

walter-nash.s: Walter Nash was a British-born New Zealand politician who was Prime Minister from 1957 to 1960, leading the Second Labour Government. As finance minister from 1935 to 1949 he had helped build the welfare state of the First Labour Government.

whina-cooper.s: Whina Cooper was a Māori leader from Northland, New Zealand, who founded the Māori Women's Welfare League in 1951 as its first president. At the age of 79 she led the Māori land march of 1975 from Te Hāpua in the far north to Parliament in Wellington, protesting against the…

wars-of-kappel.s: The Wars of Kappel were two religious wars between Reformed Zürich and the Catholic cantons of central Switzerland. The first, in 1529, ended without battle in the First Peace of Kappel.

wars-of-castro.s: The Wars of Castro were two conflicts over the Duchy of Castro, a Farnese fief in the Papal States north of Rome. In the first, from 1641 to 1644, Pope Urban VIII fought Odoardo Farnese, Duke of Parma, who was backed by Venice, Tuscany and Modena, and the papacy was forced to…

william-de-la-marck.s: William de la Marck, called the Boar of the Ardennes, was a nobleman of the house of La Marck who fought for control of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. In 1482 he killed Bishop Louis de Bourbon and installed his own son as bishop, starting years of factional war.

war-of-the-euboeote-succession.s: The War of the Euboeote Succession was fought from 1256 to 1258 between William II of Villehardouin, prince of Achaea, and a coalition of the lords of Euboea, Venice and Guy I de la Roche of Athens, over the succession to a lordship in Euboea. William's victory at Karydi in…

william-knox-darcy.s: William Knox D'Arcy was a British businessman, enriched by gold mining in Australia, who in 1901 obtained from Mozaffar ad-Din Shah a sixty-year concession to search for oil across most of Iran. After years of costly drilling his company struck oil at Masjed Soleyman in 1908,…

wat-arun.s: Wat Arun, the Temple of Dawn, is a Buddhist temple on the west bank of the Chao Phraya in Bangkok, in the old capital district of Thonburi. King Taksin made it his royal temple, and its great central prang, more than 70 metres high, was raised under Rama II and Rama III and…

wat-pho.s: Wat Pho is a royal Buddhist temple in Bangkok, just south of the Grand Palace. Rebuilt by Rama I and greatly enlarged by Rama III, it houses a 46-metre gilded reclining Buddha and the largest collection of Buddha images in Thailand.

wuchang-uprising.s: The Wuchang Uprising was an army mutiny in the city of Wuchang, now part of Wuhan, on 10 October 1911. Revolutionary soldiers of the New Army seized the city after their plans were discovered, and within weeks most provinces of central and southern China had declared…

wuhan.s: Wuhan is the capital of Hubei province in central China, at the confluence of the Yangtze and Han rivers. It was formed by the union of the cities of Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, where the Wuchang Uprising of 1911 began the Xinhai Revolution.

walter-vi-of-brienne.s: Walter VI of Brienne (c. 1304–1356) was a French nobleman and titular Duke of Athens, the son of Walter V, who had lost the duchy to the Catalan Company in 1311.

war-of-chioggia.s: The War of Chioggia (1378–1381) was a war between Venice and Genoa, with Hungary, Padua and Aquileia among Genoa's allies. In 1379 a Genoese fleet under Pietro Doria seized Chioggia at the edge of the Venetian lagoon, but the Venetians blockaded it there and forced its…

west-russian-volunteer-army.s: The West Russian Volunteer Army was a force formed in Courland in 1919 under Pavel Bermondt-Avalov, combining anti-Bolshevik Russian former prisoners of war with German Freikorps troops who had stayed in the Baltic. Nominally fighting the Bolsheviks, it attacked the Latvian…

william-c-gorgas.s: William C. Gorgas was a United States Army physician who, as chief sanitary officer of the Panama Canal from 1904, brought yellow fever and malaria under control by destroying the mosquitoes that carried them.

wusun.s: The Wusun were a nomadic people of Central Asia known from Chinese sources. Displaced from the Gansu region, they drove the Yuezhi from the Ili valley around 130 BCE and ruled the steppes of Zhetysu and the Tian Shan for several centuries, absorbing the Saka who remained there.

westphalia.s: Westphalia is a region of north-western Germany between the Rhine and the Weser, centred on Münster and reaching south to the Ruhr. It was originally the western part of the land of the Saxons; after 1180 the title of Duke of Westphalia passed to the archbishops of Cologne,…

wang-yirong.s: Wang Yirong was a Chinese scholar-official of the Qing dynasty and head of the Imperial Academy. In 1899 he recognised that inscriptions on 'dragon bones' sold as medicine were an ancient script, and he began collecting them, leading to the discovery of the Shang oracle bones.

wu-ding.s: Wu Ding was a king of the Shang dynasty who reigned for several decades in the thirteenth century BCE from the capital at Yinxu, near Anyang. The earliest known oracle-bone inscriptions date from his reign and record wars against the Tufang, Guifang and Qiang, royal hunts and…

wando.s: Wando is an island off the south-western tip of the Korean peninsula, in South Jeolla Province, South Korea. In 828 Jang Bogo founded the maritime garrison of Cheonghaejin there, from which he controlled trade between Silla, Tang China and Japan.

wonhyo.s: Wonhyo was a Buddhist monk and scholar of Silla, one of the most influential thinkers in Korean history. Setting out for Tang China, he is said to have turned back after realising that all things arise from the mind.

wujing-zongyao.s: The Wujing Zongyao (Complete Essentials for the Military Classics) is a Chinese military compendium compiled between 1040 and 1044 by Zeng Gongliang, Ding Du and Yang Weide on the order of Emperor Renzong of Song. Covering strategy, fortification, weapons and naval warfare, it…

willem-johannes-leyds.s: Willem Johannes Leyds was a Dutch-born lawyer who became state attorney of the South African Republic in 1884 and its state secretary from 1888 to 1898, Paul Kruger's chief adviser. He built up a professional civil service, largely staffed by Dutch officials, and was…

wu-state.s: Wu was a state of the Zhou period in the lower Yangtze region, centred on modern Suzhou, whose rulers claimed descent from Taibo, an uncle of King Wen of Zhou. It rose to power in the late sixth century BCE under King Helü, who defeated Chu at Boju in 506 BCE, and under his…

winrich-von-kniprode.s: Winrich von Kniprode was Grand Master of the Teutonic Order from 1351 to 1382, a period often regarded as the height of its power in Prussia. He strengthened its administration, finances and towns, encouraged learning among the brethren, and led the war against pagan…

wat-mahathat-sukhothai.s: Wat Mahathat is the principal temple at the centre of the old city of Sukhothai in Thailand, the kingdom's royal and religious centre. Its main chedi, crowned by a lotus-bud spire characteristic of Sukhothai architecture, is surrounded by subsidiary stupas, assembly halls and…

wat-si-chum.s: Wat Si Chum is a Buddhist temple just north of the old city of Sukhothai in Thailand. Its square mandapa encloses Phra Achana, a seated Buddha in the gesture of calling the earth to witness, about 15 metres wide at the knees and one of the largest Buddha images of the…

west-java.s: West Java is a province of Indonesia in the western part of the island of Java, with its capital at Bandung. It is the most populous province of the country and the homeland of the Sundanese people, and it covers much of the territory of the old Sunda Kingdom.
