william-blake.s: William Blake was an English poet, painter and engraver, now regarded as one of the great figures of Romanticism. Largely unrecognised in his lifetime, he combined text and image in his own illuminated books, including Songs of Innocence and of Experience.

washington-agreement-1946.s: The Washington Agreement of May 1946 settled Allied claims against Switzerland arising from its wartime dealings with Nazi Germany. Switzerland agreed to pay 250 million francs in return for the Allies giving up claims to gold acquired by the Swiss National Bank, and to…

world-health-organization.s: The World Health Organization is the specialised agency of the United Nations for international public health, founded on 7 April 1948 with its headquarters in Geneva. It sets health standards, coordinates responses to epidemics and supports national health systems.

washington-naval-treaty.s: The Washington Naval Treaty was an arms-limitation agreement signed in February 1922 by the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, France and Italy at the Washington Naval Conference. It fixed ratios for the tonnage of capital ships, giving Britain and the United States…

william-ewart-gladstone.s: William Ewart Gladstone was a British Liberal statesman who served four times as prime minister between 1868 and 1894. His governments introduced the secret ballot, state elementary education, army reform and the Third Reform Act, disestablished the Church of Ireland, and in…

west-africa-squadron.s: The West Africa Squadron was the Royal Navy force created in 1808 to suppress the Atlantic slave trade after Britain abolished it in 1807. Patrolling the West African coast from bases such as Freetown, it captured about 1,600 slave ships and freed some 150,000 Africans before…

watergate-scandal.s: The Watergate scandal was a political scandal in the United States that began with a break-in at the Democratic Party headquarters in the Watergate complex in Washington in June 1972 by men linked to President Richard Nixon's re-election campaign. Nixon's part in the cover-up,…

western-front-world-war-i.s: The Western Front was the main theatre of the First World War in western Europe, a line of trenches running about 700 kilometres from the Belgian coast to the Swiss border after the German advance was halted at the Marne in 1914. Battles such as Verdun, the Somme and…

whig-party-united-states.s: The Whig Party was a political party of the United States formed in the early 1830s by opponents of President Andrew Jackson. Led by figures such as Henry Clay and Daniel Webster, it favoured a national bank, protective tariffs and federal funding of roads and canals, won the…

whigs-british-political-party.s: The Whigs were a political faction and later party in England and Great Britain from the late seventeenth to the mid-nineteenth century. Originating among opponents of the Catholic James II in the Exclusion Crisis, they supported the Glorious Revolution and the Hanoverian…

white-monuments-of-vladimir-and-suzdal.n: White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal
white-monuments-of-vladimir-and-suzdal.s: The White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal are eight medieval churches and buildings of white limestone in and around Vladimir and Suzdal in Russia, inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. Built mainly in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, they include…

wisu.s: Wisu was the name used by Arab and Persian writers of the tenth to twelfth centuries for a northern forest people who traded furs with the Volga Bulgars, often by silent barter. They are usually identified with the Ves, a Finnic people known from the Russian chronicles around…

wang-xiong-cao-wei.s: Wang Xiong was an official of the Cao Wei state who served as inspector of You province, the north-eastern frontier region around modern Beijing. In 235 he sent the assassin Han Long, who killed the Xianbei leader Kebineng, ending the most dangerous Xianbei confederation of…

wuyuan-commandery.s: Wuyuan Commandery was a frontier commandery of Han China, created in 127 BCE on the great northern bend of the Yellow River, around modern Baotou in Inner Mongolia. Lying on the border with the steppe, it was repeatedly contested by the Xiongnu and later the Xianbei, and the…

wang-shifu.s: Wang Shifu was a Chinese playwright of the Yuan dynasty, author of The Romance of the Western Chamber, a long zaju drama of love between the scholar Zhang Sheng and Cui Yingying. Based on a Tang story, the play was one of the most popular works of Chinese literature for…

white-revolution.s: The White Revolution was a programme of reforms launched by Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi of Iran and approved by referendum in January 1963. It included land reform, the sale of state factories, profit-sharing for workers, a literacy corps and votes for women.

wetwang.s: Wetwang is a village in the Yorkshire Wolds in the East Riding of Yorkshire, England. Excavations at nearby Wetwang Slack revealed a large Iron Age cemetery of the Arras culture, and in 2001 the chariot burial of a woman, dated to around 300 BCE, was found in the village…

wahunsenacah.s: Wahunsenacah, known to the English as Powhatan, was the paramount chief of the Powhatan Confederacy in Tidewater Virginia. Inheriting six chiefdoms, he extended his rule over some 30 Algonquian-speaking peoples, governing from Werowocomoco.

werowocomoco.s: Werowocomoco was the chief town of Wahunsenacah, paramount chief of the Powhatan, on the north bank of the York River in Virginia. John Smith was brought there as a captive in 1607, and Wahunsenacah left it for a more distant seat in 1609.

welshpool.s: Welshpool is a market town in Powys, mid Wales, near the River Severn and the English border. It grew up below the castle of the princes of Powys Wenwynwyn and received a borough charter in the 13th century.

wolin.s: Wolin is a town on the island of the same name at the mouth of the Oder in north-western Poland. In the 10th to 12th centuries it was one of the largest trading towns on the Baltic, often identified with the Jomsborg and Vineta of the sagas.

willibald.s: Willibald was an Anglo-Saxon monk and pilgrim, a kinsman of Saint Boniface. He travelled to Rome and the Holy Land in the 720s, the first recorded English pilgrim there, and spent ten years at Monte Cassino.

willibaldsburg.s: The Willibaldsburg is a hilltop castle above Eichstätt in Bavaria, the residence of the prince-bishops of Eichstätt from the 14th to the 18th century. Rebuilt in Renaissance style around 1600 by Elias Holl, it held the famous garden recorded in the Hortus Eystettensis,…

wittstock.s: Wittstock is a town in the north of Brandenburg, Germany. It was the residence of the bishops of Havelberg, whose castle partly survives, and in 1636 the Swedish army won a major victory nearby at the Battle of Wittstock during the Thirty Years' War.

wurzen.s: Wurzen is a town on the Mulde east of Leipzig in Saxony, Germany. A collegiate church was founded there in 1114, and the bishops of Meissen ruled the surrounding district and built a castle in the town in the late 15th century.

wolfger-von-erla.s: Wolfger von Erla was bishop of Passau from 1191 and patriarch of Aquileia from 1204 until his death in 1218. A patron of poets, his travel accounts record a gift to Walther von der Vogelweide, and the Nibelungenlied is thought to have been composed at his court.

werner-i-of-strasbourg.s: Werner I was bishop of Strasbourg from 1001 to 1028 and a member of the early Habsburg family. A loyal supporter of Emperor Henry II, he began the Romanesque cathedral of Strasbourg in 1015.

william-of-champlitte.s: William of Champlitte was a Burgundian knight who took part in the Fourth Crusade. In 1205, with Geoffrey of Villehardouin, he conquered the western Peloponnese and became the first Prince of Achaea.

wolfgang-prince-of-anhalt-kothen.s: Wolfgang was Prince of Anhalt-Köthen and one of the first German princes to adopt the Reformation. In 1530 he signed the Augsburg Confession, and he joined the Protestant Schmalkaldic League.

wolfgang-of-regensburg.s: Wolfgang of Regensburg was a Swabian monk who became bishop of Regensburg in 972. A reformer, he separated the abbey of Saint Emmeram from the bishopric in 975, gave up territory for the new diocese of Prague, and tutored the future Emperor Henry II.

wakhan.s: The Wakhan is a high, narrow valley in north-eastern Afghanistan between the Pamirs and the Hindu Kush, inhabited mainly by Wakhi and Kyrgyz herders. A route of the ancient Silk Road towards China, it was ruled by local mirs under Badakhshan.

wilhelmine-of-bayreuth.s: Wilhelmine of Bayreuth was a Prussian princess, the favourite sister of Frederick the Great, who married Margrave Frederick of Brandenburg-Bayreuth in 1731. A composer, writer and patron, she made Bayreuth a centre of the arts, building the Margravial Opera House and…

william-the-victorious.s: William the Victorious was Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg of the house of Welf. In the division of the Welf lands in 1432 he received the territory between the Deister and the Leine, which became the Principality of Calenberg, and he later also gained Göttingen.

wigbert.s: Wigbert was an Anglo-Saxon monk who joined Saint Boniface's mission in Germany and became the first abbot of Fritzlar in Hesse. Around 780 Archbishop Lullus moved his relics to Hersfeld, whose abbey was dedicated to him.

wat-phra-that-lampang-luang.s: Wat Phra That Lampang Luang is a Buddhist temple near Lampang in northern Thailand, built within a walled enclosure on an old fortified mound. Its large gilded chedi, said to enshrine a relic of the Buddha, and its wooden open-sided halls make it one of the finest examples of…

war-of-the-luneburg-succession.s: The War of the Lüneburg Succession was fought from 1371 to 1388 after Duke William II of Lüneburg died without sons. Emperor Charles IV granted the principality to the Ascanian dukes of Saxe-Wittenberg, while the Guelph dukes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel claimed it by inheritance.

walrad-prince-of-nassau-usingen.s: Walrad was the founder of the Nassau-Usingen line, receiving Usingen in the Taunus in the partition of the Nassau-Saarbrücken lands in 1659. He made his career as a general of the Dutch Republic in the wars against Louis XIV and was raised to the rank of prince of the Empire…

wiesbaden.s: Wiesbaden is the capital of the German state of Hesse, on the right bank of the Rhine opposite Mainz. Its hot springs were used by the Romans, and under the princes of Nassau-Usingen and then as capital of the Duchy of Nassau from 1806 to 1866 it grew into one of Europe's most…

william-louis-count-of-nassau-dillenburg.s: William Louis was Count of Nassau-Dillenburg and stadtholder of Friesland from 1584, a nephew of William the Silent. With his cousin Maurice of Nassau he reformed the army of the Dutch Republic, introducing regular drill and the countermarch for continuous volley fire,…

william-iv-duke-of-bavaria.s: William IV was Duke of Bavaria from 1508 to 1550, ruling jointly with his brother Louis X from 1516. In 1516 the two dukes issued the beer ordinance later known as the Reinheitsgebot.

william-iv-grand-duke-of-luxembourg.n: William IV, Grand Duke of Luxembourg
william-iv-grand-duke-of-luxembourg.s: William IV was Grand Duke of Luxembourg from 1905 to 1912, the son of Grand Duke Adolphe of the House of Nassau-Weilburg. Having six daughters and no sons, he had the succession law changed in 1907 so that his eldest daughter, Marie-Adélaïde, could succeed him.

wizlaw-i-prince-of-rugen.s: Wizlaw I was Prince of Rügen from about 1221 until his death, ruling as a vassal of Denmark. He held the island and a strip of the Pomeranian mainland, encouraged German settlement and founded monasteries, and in 1234 granted town rights to Stralsund, which became a leading…

wilhelmstein.s: Wilhelmstein is an artificial island fortress in the Steinhuder Meer in Lower Saxony, Germany, built between 1761 and 1765 by Count William of Schaumburg-Lippe. Designed to defend his small state, it also housed his military school, where the young Gerhard von Scharnhorst was…

wibald.s: Wibald was abbot of Stavelot from 1130 and also of Corvey from 1146, and one of the leading statesmen of 12th-century Germany. He advised the emperors Lothair III, Conrad III and Frederick Barbarossa, and his collected letters are an important historical source.

western-bug.s: The Western Bug is a river of eastern Europe, about 770 kilometres long, rising in western Ukraine and flowing north along the borders of Poland with Ukraine and Belarus before joining the Narew. Its basin held the medieval lands of Volhynia and the Cherven towns, contested…

walter-egerton.s: Sir Walter Egerton was a British colonial administrator. Governor of Lagos from 1904, he became governor of the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria when the two were merged in 1906, with Lagos as capital, and promoted railway and harbour building.

wadi-hammamat.s: Wadi Hammamat is a dry valley in Egypt's Eastern Desert, on the route from Coptos on the Nile to the Red Sea coast. From predynastic times it was a route to gold mines and the Red Sea, and its quarries supplied the dark greywacke prized for statues and sarcophagi.

william-fiennes-1st-viscount-saye-and-se.n: William Fiennes, 1st Viscount Saye and Sele
william-fiennes-1st-viscount-saye-and-se.s: William Fiennes, 1st Viscount Saye and Sele, was an English nobleman and Puritan leader who opposed Charles I's prerogative taxation. He invested in colonial ventures including the Providence Island Company and the Saybrook settlement in Connecticut, which was partly named…

william-phips.s: Sir William Phips was a Maine-born shipbuilder and treasure hunter who was knighted after recovering silver from a Spanish wreck off Hispaniola in 1687. In 1690 he captured Port Royal in Acadia but failed in an attack on Quebec.

william-light.s: William Light was a British army officer and surveyor, the first Surveyor-General of South Australia. Born in Penang, the son of its founder Francis Light, he served in the Peninsular War before sailing to South Australia in 1836.

william-mcdougall.s: William McDougall was a Canadian politician and Father of Confederation who, as a federal minister, negotiated the transfer of Rupert's Land to Canada. Appointed lieutenant governor of the North-West Territories in 1869, he was turned back by armed Métis at the border of the…

willamette-valley.s: The Willamette Valley is a fertile valley about 240 km long in north-western Oregon, United States, drained by the Willamette River between the Cascade Range and the Coast Range. Retired fur traders and missionaries farmed it from the 1830s, and it was the main destination of…

wang-xianzhi.s: Wang Xianzhi was a salt smuggler who led one of the great rebellions against the late Tang dynasty. Rising in 874 or 875 amid famine and heavy taxes, he was joined by Huang Chao and raided widely between the Yellow River and the Huai.

wat-phra-kaew.s: Wat Phra Kaew, the Temple of the Emerald Buddha, is the royal temple within the Grand Palace in Bangkok. Built by King Rama I from 1782 and consecrated in 1784, it houses the Emerald Buddha, the most venerated image in Thailand, whose robes the king changes with the seasons…

waldheim-affair.s: The Waldheim affair was a controversy over the wartime past of Kurt Waldheim, former Secretary-General of the United Nations, during his successful campaign for the Austrian presidency in 1986. Revelations showed that he had concealed his service as a Wehrmacht officer in the…

welf-vi.s: Welf VI was a German prince of the Welf dynasty who held the Matildine lands, the March of Tuscany and the Duchy of Spoleto from 1152, granted by his nephew Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. He was also an uncle of Henry the Lion and ruled the family's lands in Swabia.

war-of-the-supremes.s: The War of the Supremes was a civil war in the Republic of New Granada, present-day Colombia and Panama, from 1839 to 1842. It began as a revolt in Pasto against the closure of small convents and spread as regional strongmen, the 'supreme chiefs', rose against the government…

washington-on-the-brazos.s: Washington-on-the-Brazos is a small community on the Brazos River in Texas where delegates to the Convention of 1836 declared Texas independent from Mexico on 2 March 1836 and drafted its constitution. It later served as the seat of government of the Republic of Texas in the…

wiskiauten.s: Wiskiauten, now Mokhovoye in Russia's Kaliningrad region, is an archaeological site on the Sambian peninsula near the Curonian Lagoon. Its burial ground of several hundred mounds held Scandinavian-style graves of the 9th to 11th centuries, showing that Scandinavian traders…

wonjong-of-goryeo.s: Wonjong was king of Goryeo in Korea from 1260 to 1274. As crown prince he travelled to submit to the Mongols and met Kublai, whose support helped him to the throne.

wends.s: Wends is a historical name used by Germans and others for Slavic peoples living near Germanic lands, especially between the Elbe and the Oder. The Chronicle of Fredegar applies it to the Slavs led by Samo in the 7th century, and in the Middle Ages it chiefly meant the Polabian…

widukind.s: Widukind was a Westphalian nobleman who led Saxon resistance to Charlemagne in the Saxon Wars. Taking refuge with the Danes when the Franks advanced, he returned to lead repeated revolts, including the victory at the Süntel in 782 that was followed by Charlemagne's massacre of…

warwick-patent.s: The Warwick Patent was a grant of land in southern New England issued in 1632 (1631 in the old-style calendar) by Robert Rich, 2nd Earl of Warwick, as president of the Council for New England. Its holders, a group of Puritan lords and gentlemen led by Viscount Saye and Sele…

wewoka-oklahoma.s: Wewoka is a town in central Oklahoma, founded in 1849 by Black Seminoles led by John Horse. It became the capital of the Seminole Nation in Indian Territory and remains the seat of Seminole County.

wisnuwardhana.s: Wisnuwardhana was king of Singhasari in eastern Java from about 1248 until his death in 1268. According to the Pararaton he ended a cycle of murders among the descendants of Ken Arok and ruled jointly with his cousin Mahisa Campaka.

walter-raleigh.s: Walter Raleigh (c. 1552–1618) was an English courtier, soldier, explorer and writer, a favourite of Elizabeth I.

war-of-the-league.s: The War of the League was a brief civil war in Costa Rica in September and October 1835. Cartago, Alajuela and Heredia formed a league against San José after the repeal of the law that had rotated the seat of government among the towns, leaving San José as the capital.

wu-geng.s: Wu Geng, also called Lufu, was a son of the last Shang king. After the Zhou conquest around 1046 BCE he was left to rule the Shang heartland under the watch of King Wu's brothers.

war-of-the-knives.s: The War of the Knives was a civil war in Saint-Domingue in 1799–1800 between Toussaint Louverture, who controlled the north and west, and André Rigaud, leader of the free people of colour in the south. Toussaint's forces under Jean-Jacques Dessalines overran the south, and…

wang-ben.s: Wang Ben was a general of the State of Qin, son of the general Wang Jian, active in the wars of unification under King Zheng. In 225 BCE he took the Wei capital Daliang by flooding it, and he then destroyed the last Yan forces in Liaodong and, in 221 BCE, occupied the State of…

wu-qi.s: Wu Qi was a general and reformer of the Warring States period, born in the State of Wey. He commanded the armies of Wei under Marquis Wen, winning the lands west of the Yellow River from Qin, and later served King Dao of Chu as chief minister, cutting the privileges of the…

wu-zixu.s: Wu Zixu was a minister and general of the State of Wu, originally from Chu, who fled to Wu after the Chu king killed his father and brother in 522 BCE. He helped Helü seize the throne and led the campaign that took the Chu capital Ying in 506 BCE, where tradition says he…

wu-taibo.s: Taibo was, in Chinese tradition, the eldest son of the Zhou chieftain Gugong Danfu and an uncle of King Wen of Zhou. With his brother Zhongyong he withdrew to the lower Yangtze so that their younger brother Jili and his son could inherit, adopted local customs and founded the…

wen-zhong.s: Wen Zhong was a minister of King Goujian of Yue in the 5th century BCE. With Fan Li he guided Yue's recovery after its defeat by Wu in 494 BCE and its conquest of Wu in 473 BCE, reportedly devising a set of stratagems to weaken Wu.

wafd-party.s: The Wafd was an Egyptian nationalist party that grew out of the delegation (wafd) led by Saad Zaghloul in 1918 to demand independence from Britain. The most popular party of the monarchy, it won most free elections between 1924 and 1950 and negotiated the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty…

wilhelm-junker.s: Wilhelm Junker was a Russian-born explorer of German descent who travelled widely in north-central Africa. Between 1879 and 1886 he explored the Uele and Mbomou basins and the lands of the Zande and Mangbetu, staying with rulers such as Zemio.

wismar-tribunal.s: The Wismar Tribunal was the supreme court of appeal for Sweden's German possessions, including Swedish Pomerania, Bremen-Verden and Wismar, set up at Wismar in 1653. It replaced appeals to the courts of the Holy Roman Empire, which Sweden's territories were exempted from under…

wasusarma.s: Wasusarma was a king of Tabal in south-central Anatolia in the 8th century BCE, son of Tuwati. He paid tribute to the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III, but around 730 BCE was deposed for withholding it and replaced by a commoner named Hulli.

wiwa-people.s: The Wiwa are an Indigenous people of the south-eastern and eastern slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in northern Colombia, one of the four peoples regarded as heirs of the Tairona. They speak a Chibchan language, Damana, and share with the Kogi, Arhuaco and Kankuamo a…

wushe-incident.s: The Wushe Incident (Musha Incident) was an uprising of Seediq people against Japanese colonial rule at Wushe (Musha) in central Taiwan in October 1930. Led by the chief Mona Rudao, warriors attacked a school sports meeting and killed more than 130 Japanese.

wangsakerta-manuscripts.s: The Wangsakerta manuscripts are a group of texts on the history of Java and the Indonesian archipelago attributed to Prince Wangsakerta of Cirebon in the late 17th century. They give detailed lists of kings and dates, including for Tarumanagara, but came to light only in the…

william-henry-harrison.s: William Henry Harrison was an American soldier and politician, governor of Indiana Territory from 1801 to 1812 and the ninth president of the United States. As governor he pressed land cessions on Native nations, defeated Tenskwatawa's warriors at Tippecanoe in 1811 and beat…

wolde-selassie.s: Wolde Selassie was the ruler of Tigray, in northern Ethiopia, from about 1790 until his death in 1816, during the Era of Princes. From his seat at Antalo he was one of the most powerful lords in the country.

wube-haile-maryam.s: Wube Haile Maryam was the lord of Semien who also ruled Tigray from 1831 to 1855, making him one of the strongest regional rulers of the Ethiopian Era of Princes. He sought European contacts and firearms to strengthen his position.

wilfrid-malleson.s: Wilfrid Malleson was a British Indian Army general who in 1918 led a military mission from Meshed in north-eastern Persia to support the anti-Bolshevik Transcaspian Government. His small force of Indian and British troops fought Red Army units along the Trans-Caspian railway,…

wuzhile.s: Wuzhile was the founder of Turgesh power in Central Asia. A chief of the Turgesh tribes, he took the city of Suyab around 699 as the Western Turkic Khaganate disintegrated, and he built up a realm in the valleys of the Chu and Ili rivers.

warpalawa.s: Warpalawa was king of Tuwana, a Neo-Hittite kingdom in southern Cappadocia, in the second half of the 8th century BCE. Assyrian records name him as Urballa among the rulers who paid tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III.

walter-reed.s: Walter Reed was a United States Army physician who in 1900 led the commission in Cuba that proved Carlos Finlay's theory that yellow fever is spread by mosquitoes. Experiments with human volunteers at Camp Lazear near Havana established the mode of transmission, allowing the…

wesley-merritt.s: Wesley Merritt was a United States Army general who served as a cavalry commander in the American Civil War and later in the wars against Native Americans of the West. In 1898 he commanded the expedition to the Philippines during the Spanish–American War, took Manila in August…

william-mckinley.s: William McKinley was the 25th President of the United States, from 1897 until his assassination in 1901. A Republican from Ohio, he led the country in the Spanish–American War of 1898, which brought the annexation of Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, and he also annexed…

waikato.s: The Waikato is a region in the north of New Zealand's North Island, named after the Waikato River, the country's longest. It is the home of the Waikato–Tainui iwi, whose chief Pōtatau Te Wherowhero became the first Māori King in 1858.

waitangi-northland.s: Waitangi is a locality in the Bay of Islands in Northland, New Zealand, where the British Resident James Busby built his house in 1833–1834. There northern Māori chiefs signed the Declaration of the Independence of New Zealand in 1835, and on 6 February 1840 the Treaty of…

william-lyon-mackenzie.s: William Lyon Mackenzie was a Scottish-born journalist and politician in Upper Canada, a radical critic of the ruling Family Compact and the first mayor of Toronto in 1834. In December 1837 he led a short-lived armed rebellion near Toronto, which was quickly defeated.

warka-vase.s: The Warka Vase is a carved alabaster vessel about one metre tall, found in the Eanna precinct at Uruk (modern Warka) in Iraq and dated to about 3200–3000 BCE. Its bands of relief show water, plants, animals, naked men carrying offerings and a procession to the goddess Inanna,…

warrior-of-capestrano.s: The Warrior of Capestrano is a limestone statue of a warrior, more than two metres tall, found in 1934 in a cemetery at Capestrano in Abruzzo, Italy. Made in the 6th century BCE, it shows a man in a broad-brimmed hat with breastplate, sword and axe.

wawat.s: Wawat was the ancient Egyptian name for Lower Nubia, the Nile valley between the First and Second Cataracts. Egypt raided, fortified and exploited it from the Old and Middle Kingdoms for gold, stone and trade goods, and under the New Kingdom it formed one of the two provinces…

wallia.s: Wallia was king of the Visigoths from 415 to 418. After a failed attempt to cross to Africa, he made peace with Rome, returned the captive Galla Placidia and fought for the empire in Hispania, destroying the Siling Vandals and crushing the Alans.

wawel-hill.s: Wawel is a limestone hill on the left bank of the Vistula in Kraków, southern Poland. A fortified centre of the Vistulans in the early Middle Ages, it became the seat of Polish rulers, with the Royal Castle, rebuilt in Renaissance style by Italian architects in the early 16th…

wislica.s: Wiślica is a small town on the Nida in the Świętokrzyskie region of southern Poland. An early medieval stronghold, possibly a centre of the Vistulans, it became an important ducal seat under the Piasts, and its Romanesque church preserves an engraved gypsum floor of the late…

wa-na.s: Wa Na is the title of the paramount chief of Wa, a Wala kingdom in the Upper West Region of Ghana. The office rotates among several royal gates, or branches of the ruling family, and the chief rules alongside Muslim office-holders and earth-priests who keep the rites of the land.

wampanoag-tribe-of-gay-head-aquinnah.s: The Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) is a Native American tribe based at Aquinnah, formerly Gay Head, at the western end of Martha's Vineyard in Massachusetts. Its members descend from the Wampanoag communities of the island, who kept part of their land through the…

wamsutta.s: Wamsutta, called Alexander by the English, was the eldest son of Massasoit and became sachem of the Wampanoag after his father's death around 1661. In 1662 Plymouth Colony, suspicious of his land sales and dealings, had him brought in under armed escort for questioning, and he…

wassoulou.s: Wassoulou is a savanna region on the borders of southern Mali, north-eastern Guinea and north-western Côte d'Ivoire, around the upper Sankarani River. Its people, largely of Fula origin but speaking the Maninka language, gave their name to the Wassoulou Empire founded by…

washington-naval-conference.s: The Washington Naval Conference was an international meeting held in Washington from November 1921 to February 1922 on naval disarmament and the Pacific. Its treaties limited the battleship fleets of Britain, the United States, Japan, France and Italy, replaced the…

wabash-river.s: The Wabash River flows about 810 kilometres from western Ohio across Indiana to the Ohio River, forming part of the border between Indiana and Illinois. Its valley was home to the Miami and other Native peoples and was settled by the French at Vincennes.

walmu.s: Walmu was a king of Wilusa in north-western Anatolia in the late 13th century BCE. He is known from the so-called Milawata letter, written by a Hittite king, probably Tudhaliya IV, which records that Walmu had been driven out of Wilusa and that the Hittites intended to restore…

witu.s: Witu is a town in Lamu County on the coast of Kenya, north-west of Lamu Island. It became the fortified capital of the sultanate of Witu, founded around 1860 by Ahmad Simba of the Nabhani family after he fled the forces of Zanzibar.

wang-zhengjun.s: Wang Zhengjun (71 BCE–13 CE) was empress to Emperor Yuan of Han and, as empress dowager and grand empress dowager, a dominant figure at the Han court for more than six decades. Her relatives of the Wang clan filled the highest offices, and she promoted her nephew Wang Mang as…

wagshum.s: Wagshum was the hereditary title of the rulers of Wag, a district of Lasta in northern Ethiopia, whose family claimed descent from the Zagwe dynasty. The wagshums were among the great regional lords of the Ethiopian Empire, and one of them, Gobeze, ruled as Emperor Tekle…

wasit.s: Wasit was a city in central Iraq on the Tigris, founded around 702 by the Umayyad governor al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf as the garrison and administrative capital of Iraq, midway between Kufa and Basra. It remained an important provincial centre under the Abbasids and later dynasties,…

wagang-army.s: The Wagang Army was one of the largest rebel forces in the collapse of the Sui dynasty, named after its base at Wagang in Henan. Founded by Zhai Rang around 611 and led from 617 by Li Mi, it seized the granaries near Luoyang and dominated the central plain, but was crushed by…

wars-of-alexander-the-great.s: The Wars of Alexander the Great were the campaigns fought by Alexander III of Macedon between 336 and 323 BCE, first to secure Greece and then against the Achaemenid Persian Empire. Victories at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela gave him Anatolia, Egypt, Mesopotamia and Iran,…

war-of-the-seventh-coalition.s: The War of the Seventh Coalition was the final campaign of the Napoleonic Wars, fought in 1815 after Napoleon escaped from Elba and retook power in France during the Hundred Days. Britain, Prussia, Austria, Russia and other states united against him, and his defeat at Waterloo…

war-of-the-first-coalition.s: The War of the First Coalition (1792–1797) was the first of the French Revolutionary Wars, fought by revolutionary France against Austria, Prussia, Britain, Spain, the Dutch Republic, Sardinia and other states. After early setbacks France conquered the Austrian Netherlands and…

war-of-the-third-coalition.s: The War of the Third Coalition (1805) was fought by Napoleonic France and its allies against Britain, Austria, Russia, Sweden and Naples. war-of-the-quadruple-alliance.s: The War of the Quadruple Alliance (1718–1720) was fought by Britain, France, Austria and the Dutch Republic against Spain, which under Philip V and his minister Giulio Alberoni had seized Sardinia and Sicily in defiance of the Utrecht settlement. The British fleet destroyed…

war-of-the-sixth-coalition.s: The War of the Sixth Coalition (1813–1814) was fought, after Napoleon's disastrous invasion of Russia, by Russia, Prussia, Austria, Britain, Sweden and other states against France. Napoleon won several battles in Germany in 1813 but was decisively beaten at Leipzig in October,…

war-of-the-fourth-coalition.s: The War of the Fourth Coalition (1806–1807) was fought by Napoleonic France against Prussia, Russia, Saxony, Sweden and Britain. Napoleon crushed the Prussian army at Jena and Auerstedt in October 1806 and occupied Berlin, then fought the Russians at Eylau and defeated them at…

wadai-war.s: The Wadai War was the French conquest of the Sultanate of Wadai in present-day eastern Chad. French troops took the capital Abéché in 1909 and drove out Sultan Dud Murra, who fought on with support from the neighbouring Masalit sultanate.

war-of-the-pacific.s: The War of the Pacific was fought from 1879 to 1884 between Chile and an alliance of Bolivia and Peru over the nitrate-rich Atacama coast. Chile won at sea and on land and occupied Lima in 1881; it took Tarapacá from Peru and the coastal province of Antofagasta from Bolivia,…

williamite-war-in-ireland.s: The Williamite War in Ireland was fought from 1688 to 1691 between the supporters of the deposed Catholic king James II and those of William III, who had replaced him in the Glorious Revolution. William's victories at the Boyne (1690) and Aughrim (1691) and the surrender of…

war-of-the-league-of-cambrai.n: War of the League of Cambrai
war-of-the-league-of-cambrai.s: The War of the League of Cambrai was fought from 1508 to 1516 during the Italian Wars. It began when Pope Julius II, Louis XII of France, Emperor Maximilian I and Ferdinand of Aragon allied against Venice, which was routed at Agnadello in 1509; the alliances then shifted…

war-of-the-league-of-cognac.n: War of the League of Cognac
war-of-the-league-of-cognac.s: The War of the League of Cognac was fought from 1526 to 1530 between Emperor Charles V and an alliance of France, Pope Clement VII, Venice, Florence and Milan formed to limit Habsburg power in Italy. Imperial troops sacked Rome in 1527, and the Peace of Cambrai (1529) and the…

war-of-the-fifth-coalition.s: The War of the Fifth Coalition was fought in 1809 between Napoleonic France and its allies and Austria, supported by Britain. Austria invaded Bavaria and won at Aspern-Essling in May, Napoleon's first major personal defeat, but lost at Wagram in July; by the Treaty of…

war-in-afghanistan-2001-2021.s: The War in Afghanistan was fought from 2001 to 2021 after the United States and its allies invaded Afghanistan following the attacks of 11 September 2001 and overthrew the Taliban government that sheltered al-Qaeda. wars-in-lombardy.s: The Wars in Lombardy were a series of conflicts from 1423 to 1454 between the Republic of Venice and the Duchy of Milan, with Florence and other Italian states drawn in. Fought largely by condottieri such as Carmagnola, Gattamelata and Francesco Sforza, they extended Venice's…

winter-war.s: The Winter War was fought between the Soviet Union and Finland from November 1939 to March 1940, after Finland refused Soviet demands for territory. Finnish forces inflicted heavy losses on the much larger Red Army, but the Moscow Peace Treaty of March 1940 forced Finland to…

war-of-the-polish-succession.s: The War of the Polish Succession was fought from 1733 to 1735 over the succession to Augustus II of Poland. Russia and Austria backed Augustus III against Stanisław Leszczyński, supported by France, Spain and Sardinia; Augustus won the Polish throne, while the Treaty of Vienna…

war-of-1812.s: The War of 1812 was fought from 1812 to 1815 between the United States and the United Kingdom, with Britain's Canadian colonies and Native American allies. Provoked by British trade restrictions and the impressment of American sailors, it saw failed American invasions of…

war-of-devolution.s: The War of Devolution was fought in 1667–1668 between France and Spain over the Spanish Netherlands. Louis XIV claimed parts of it for his wife Maria Theresa under a local inheritance law, the 'right of devolution', and quickly overran much of Flanders and Franche-Comté;…

war-of-the-brabantine-succession.s: The War of the Brabantine Succession was fought in 1356–1357 over the inheritance of Duke John III of Brabant, whose daughter Joanna and her husband Wenceslaus succeeded him. Louis of Male, Count of Flanders, claimed part of the duchy, defeated the Brabançons at Scheut in 1356…

war-of-the-castilian-succession.s: The War of the Castilian Succession was fought from 1475 to 1479 over the crown of Castile after the death of Henry IV. Supporters of his daughter Joanna la Beltraneja, backed by Afonso V of Portugal, fought those of his half-sister Isabella I and her husband Ferdinand of Aragon.

war-of-the-flemish-succession.s: The War of the Flemish Succession was a conflict over the succession to Margaret II, Countess of Flanders and Hainaut, between her sons from two marriages, the Avesnes and the Dampierre. William of Holland backed the Avesnes and defeated the Dampierre and French forces at…

war-of-the-remences.s: The War of the Remences was a series of peasant risings in fifteenth-century Catalonia by the remences, serfs who owed payments to redeem themselves from their lords. They fought alongside John II during the Catalan Civil War and rose again in 1484 under Pere Joan Sala.

wars-of-the-three-kingdoms.s: The Wars of the Three Kingdoms were a series of linked wars from 1639 to 1653 in England, Scotland and Ireland, then ruled by Charles I. They included the Bishops' Wars, the Irish Confederate Wars and the English Civil War, fought over religion, royal power and the relations…

war-of-the-confederation.s: The War of the Confederation was fought from 1836 to 1839 by Chile, with Peruvian exiles and Argentine support, against the Peru–Bolivian Confederation created by the Bolivian president Andrés de Santa Cruz. After a failed first Chilean expedition, the Chilean general Manuel…

war-of-the-burgundian-succession.s: The War of the Burgundian Succession was fought from 1477 to 1482 over the lands of Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, who died at Nancy. Louis XI of France seized the duchy of Burgundy and other lands, while Charles's daughter Mary and her husband Maximilian of Austria…

war-of-the-portuguese-succession.s: The War of the Portuguese Succession followed the death of the childless Cardinal-King Henry in 1580. Philip II of Spain claimed the throne, and his army under the Duke of Alba defeated the pretender António, Prior of Crato, at Alcântara near Lisbon in August 1580.
